formal: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, published in 2009, was designed to help systematic reviewers transparently report why the review was done, what the authors did, and what they found. Over the past decade, advances in systematic review methodology and terminology have necessitated an update to the guideline. The PRISMA 2020 statement replaces the 2009 statement and includes new reporting guidance that reflects advances in methods to identify, select, appraise, and synthesise studies. The structure and presentation of the items have been modified to facilitate implementation. In this article, we present the PRISMA 2020 27-item checklist, an expanded checklist that details reporting recommendations for each item, the PRISMA 2020 abstract checklist, and the revised flow diagrams for original and updated reviews.
casual: Okay, so basically, the PRISMA statement – which came out in 2009 – was created to make sure people doing systematic reviews really clearly explain *why* they were doing them, exactly what they did, and what their results showed. But over time, things have changed a lot in how we do these kinds of reviews, so it needed an update! The PRISMA 2020 version is now the one to use, and it's got new advice on everything from finding studies and checking them carefully to actually putting all the information together. They’ve also made the checklist easier to follow. We’re going to walk you through the whole thing – the 27-item checklist itself, a detailed breakdown for each item, the abstract checklist, and the updated flow diagrams for both new and revised reviews.

formal: SciPy is an open-source scientific computing library for the Python programming language. Since its initial release in 2001, SciPy has become a de facto standard for leveraging scientific algorithms in Python, with over 600 unique code contributors, thousands of dependent packages, over 100,000 dependent repositories and millions of downloads per year. In this work, we provide an overview of the capabilities and development practices of SciPy 1.0 and highlight some recent technical developments.
casual: Okay, so basically, SciPy is this awesome, free library you can use with Python if you’re doing any kind of serious science or math stuff. It's become super popular – like, a really big deal! Since it came out back in 2001, over 600 different people have helped write code for it, and there are tons of other programs that rely on it. Seriously, there are more than 100,000 repositories linked to SciPy, and it gets downloaded by millions of people every year. This paper is going to give us a look at what SciPy 1.0 could do, plus some newer stuff they've been working on.

formal: Radiation resistant camera system was constructed for monitoring deuterium plasma discharges in the Large Helical Device (LHD). This system has contributed to safe operation during two experimental campaigns without serious problems due to radiation (neutrons and gamma-rays). The cameras steadily functioned even in the plasma discharge with the maximum neutron emission rate in FY 2017, though some bright specks temporarily appeared on the images. The cameras have been installed in shield boxes which consist of lead boxes covered with 10% borated polyethylene blocks in all directions. For optimizing the design of the shield box, the radiation flux distribution was calculated by MCNP-6 code, which reveals the reduction of the radiation flux and the change of the energy spectra in the shield box. Thanks to the optimization, significant extension of the lifetime of the cameras has been realized. Investigation of the influence of the radiation on the CCD image sensor shows that the number of bright specks generally increases with the radiation flux to the camera, which also indicates that some bright specks disappear by the self-annealing process on the image sensor. This phenomenon also highly contributes to the further extension of the lifetime of the radiation resistant cameras.
casual:
Okay, so basically, they built a super tough camera system to watch deuterium plasma in the LHD – that’s a big fusion experiment! It's helped them run experiments safely for two campaigns now, without any serious issues caused by radiation like neutrons and gamma rays. The cameras themselves kept working fine, even when the plasma was pumping out *tons* of neutrons back in 2017 – although you'd sometimes see a little bit of bright fuzz on the pictures.

These cameras are housed in these really thick shield boxes: they’re basically lead boxes wrapped with blocks of plastic that contain boron, all around! They used a computer program called MCNP-6 to figure out exactly how the radiation was spreading inside those boxes and it helped them design the shields to be even better. This made the radiation much weaker where the cameras were, which is why the cameras are lasting so much longer.

They studied how the radiation affects the camera’s sensors, and they found that more bright spots appeared as the radiation got stronger – like tiny bubbles popping on a hot screen! But some of those spots actually disappeared over time too, kind of like they “healed” themselves. That's also helping to make the cameras last even longer, which is pretty cool!

formal: As a present to Mizar on its 50th anniversary, we develop an AI/TP system that automatically proves about 60% of the Mizar theorems in the hammer setting. We also automatically prove 75% of the Mizar theorems when the automated provers are helped by using only the premises used in the human-written Mizar proofs. We describe the methods and large-scale experiments leading to these results. This includes in particular the E and Vampire provers, their ENIGMA and Deepire learning modifications, a number of learning-based premise selection methods, and the incremental loop that interleaves growing a corpus of millions of ATP proofs with training increasingly strong AI/TP systems on them. We also present a selection of Mizar problems that were proved automatically.
casual: Okay, so to celebrate Mizar’s 50th anniversary, we built this really cool AI and theorem-proving system – let's call it an AI/TP thing. It basically figured out about 60% of all the theorems in Mizar when you just let it go wild on its own (we call that the “hammer setting”). But here’s the even better part: if we gave it a little help, like telling it to only use the original human-written proofs as clues, it could solve 75% of those same theorems! We've written up all about how we did this, including details on some powerful provers called E and Vampire. Plus, we tweaked them with AI learning – specifically ENIGMA and Deepire – and used a bunch of clever ways to pick the best premises for the AI to look at. It’s like we were building this massive collection of automated theorem proofs (millions of ATP proofs!), while also training these super-smart AI/TP systems on them, all in an ongoing loop. We even picked out some specific Mizar problems that the system successfully solved automatically – pretty neat, right?

formal: While the Transformer architecture has become the de-facto standard for natural language processing tasks, its applications to computer vision remain limited. In vision, attention is either applied in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used to replace certain components of convolutional networks while keeping their overall structure in place. We show that this reliance on CNNs is not necessary and a pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification tasks. When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB, etc.), Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.
casual: Okay, so basically, the Transformer – it’s now *super* popular for things like understanding language. But when we try to use it with pictures, it hasn't really taken off yet. Usually, people add attention (a part of Transformers) to regular CNNs, or they just swap out some parts of a CNN with attention, but keep the whole thing looking similar. What’s cool is that we found you don't *need* CNNs at all! If you just use a Transformer directly on groups of picture patches—that’s what ViT does—it actually works really well for figuring out what pictures are. We trained it on tons of data and then tested it on things like ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and VTAB, and it beat the best CNNs while using way less computer power to learn.

formal: Since the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) 18 years ago, a large number of SARS-related coronaviruses (SARSr-CoVs) have been discovered in their natural reservoir host, bats<sup>1-4</sup>. Previous studies have shown that some bat SARSr-CoVs have the potential to infect humans<sup>5-7</sup>. Here we report the identification and characterization of a new coronavirus (2019-nCoV), which caused an epidemic of acute respiratory syndrome in humans in Wuhan, China. The epidemic, which started on 12 December 2019, had caused 2,794 laboratory-confirmed infections including 80 deaths by 26 January 2020. Full-length genome sequences were obtained from five patients at an early stage of the outbreak. The sequences are almost identical and share 79.6% sequence identity to SARS-CoV. Furthermore, we show that 2019-nCoV is 96% identical at the whole-genome level to a bat coronavirus. Pairwise protein sequence analysis of seven conserved non-structural proteins domains show that this virus belongs to the species of SARSr-CoV. In addition, 2019-nCoV virus isolated from the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of a critically ill patient could be neutralized by sera from several patients. Notably, we confirmed that 2019-nCoV uses the same cell entry receptor-angiotensin converting enzyme II (ACE2)-as SARS-CoV.
casual:
Okay, so basically, way back in 2003 with the SARS outbreak, scientists started finding tons of related coronaviruses – we call them SARSr-CoVs – living in bats<sup style="vertical-align:middle">1-4</sup>. Turns out, some of these bat viruses could actually jump over to infect people<sup style="vertical-align:middle">5-7</sup>.

Recently, they found a brand new coronavirus, which they’ve named 2019-nCoV. This thing caused a huge outbreak of sickness in humans – like, a really bad respiratory illness – starting in Wuhan, China back on December 12th, 2019. By January 26th, 2020, they’d confirmed over 2,794 infections, and sadly, 80 people had died.

They got the complete genetic code from five patients really early in the outbreak, and guess what? The sequences were almost exactly the same! They're about 79.6% similar to another coronavirus called SARS-CoV. It’s also super close to bats – like 96% identical at the whole genome level.

They even looked at the proteins within the virus and found that it fits right into the “SARSr-CoV” family. Plus, they discovered that this 2019-nCoV could be stopped by antibodies from people who had been infected. And here's the important part: just like SARS-CoV, this new virus uses a protein called ACE2 to get inside our cells – that’s how it starts infecting us!

formal: Array programming provides a powerful, compact and expressive syntax for accessing, manipulating and operating on data in vectors, matrices and higher-dimensional arrays. NumPy is the primary array programming library for the Python language. It has an essential role in research analysis pipelines in fields as diverse as physics, chemistry, astronomy, geoscience, biology, psychology, materials science, engineering, finance and economics. For example, in astronomy, NumPy was an important part of the software stack used in the discovery of gravitational waves<sup>1</sup> and in the first imaging of a black hole<sup>2</sup>. Here we review how a few fundamental array concepts lead to a simple and powerful programming paradigm for organizing, exploring and analysing scientific data. NumPy is the foundation upon which the scientific Python ecosystem is constructed. It is so pervasive that several projects, targeting audiences with specialized needs, have developed their own NumPy-like interfaces and array objects. Owing to its central position in the ecosystem, NumPy increasingly acts as an interoperability layer between such array computation libraries and, together with its application programming interface (API), provides a flexible framework to support the next decade of scientific and industrial analysis.
casual:
Okay, so basically, “array programming” is a really cool way to work with numbers – like big sets of them organized into things called vectors, matrices, and even arrays with more dimensions. It lets you easily grab data, change it around, and do all sorts of calculations on it. NumPy is the main tool for this in Python. Seriously, it’s super important! You find it used everywhere—like in physics, chemistry, astronomy, geology, biology, psychology – basically any science field you can think of, plus finance and economics too.

Think about it: it was a huge part of how scientists figured out about gravitational waves and even took the very first picture of a black hole!  NumPy is like the base for all the other cool tools in Python for science. Lots of different projects have built things that are kind of like NumPy, but it’s still the main one. Because it's so popular, it helps connect different programs together and offers a really flexible way to do analysis now and probably for years to come—it’s super important for both scientific research and even industry!

formal: In recent times, researchers across various fields have become interested in the topic of fractional calculus based on integrals and derivatives of fractional order. This area has numerous and widespread applications in fields of science and engineering, including wave and fluid dynamics, mathematical biology, financial systems, structural dynamics, robotics, and artificial intelligence, among others. Therefore, fractional models have become relevant in the context of phenomena with memory effects, in place of the conventional reliance on ordinary or partial differential equations. Fractional calculus offers superior tools for addressing time-dependent effects compared to integer-order calculus, which forms the foundation of most mathematical systems. As a result, fractional calculus is crucial to modeling real-life problems, and finding mathematical solutions is a great challenge in this regard.
casual: Okay, so lately, scientists have been really digging into something called fractional calculus – basically, it’s about integrals and derivatives that aren't just whole numbers like 1 or 2. It’s actually turning out to be super useful in tons of different areas, like how waves and fluids move, how living things work mathematically, even with money markets, building designs, robots, and AI! So, people are using these “fractional models” because they're better at describing stuff that has a kind of memory – you know, where the past still affects what’s happening now. Regular calculus (the kind we usually use) isn’t always great at handling things that change over time. It’s actually way more powerful than regular math for figuring out real-world problems, but it's also really tricky to solve those equations!

formal: Abstract The Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis (MEGA) software has matured to contain a large collection of methods and tools of computational molecular evolution. Here, we describe new additions that make MEGA a more comprehensive tool for building timetrees of species, pathogens, and gene families using rapid relaxed-clock methods. Methods for estimating divergence times and confidence intervals are implemented to use probability densities for calibration constraints for node-dating and sequence sampling dates for tip-dating analyses. They are supported by new options for tagging sequences with spatiotemporal sampling information, an expanded interactive Node Calibrations Editor, and an extended Tree Explorer to display timetrees. Also added is a Bayesian method for estimating neutral evolutionary probabilities of alleles in a species using multispecies sequence alignments and a machine learning method to test for the autocorrelation of evolutionary rates in phylogenies. The computer memory requirements for the maximum likelihood analysis are reduced significantly through reprogramming, and the graphical user interface has been made more responsive and interactive for very big data sets. These enhancements will improve the user experience, quality of results, and the pace of biological discovery. Natively compiled graphical user interface and command-line versions of MEGA11 are available for Microsoft Windows, Linux, and macOS from www.megasoftware.net.
casual:
Okay, so basically, MEGA software has gotten a huge upgrade! It’s now packed with tons of cool tools to study how genes and species have evolved. We've added some new stuff that makes it way better for building these “timetrees” – you know, trees showing when different species, viruses, or gene families split off from each other.

Here's the breakdown: Now, MEGA can really quickly figure out how long things have been evolving using a new method called “relaxed-clock.” It’s all about estimating those dates and figuring out just how sure we are about them, using probabilities to help pinpoint when branches started and ended. Plus, you can now easily label your sequences with information about where and when they were sampled – it's way more organized!

We also have a new interactive tool for setting up the calibration points for those timetrees, and the Tree Explorer has been expanded so you can see everything really clearly. There’s even a Bayesian method to figure out how likely different versions of genes are to have evolved in different species, using multiple DNA sequences. And we've added a machine learning trick to check if evolutionary rates tend to repeat themselves within a family tree.

To top it off, MEGA is now way faster and uses less computer memory – especially when doing maximum likelihood analyses! The interface is also much smoother and easier to use, even with really big datasets. All of these changes should make it easier for scientists to get accurate results and speed up their research. 

You can download the latest version (MEGA11) for Windows, Linux, or macOS from www.megasoftware.net – it’s natively compiled so it runs super smoothly!

formal: On the basis of this information, there is evidence that human-to-human transmission has occurred among close contacts since the middle of December 2019. Considerable efforts to reduce transmission will be required to control outbreaks if similar dynamics apply elsewhere. Measures to prevent or reduce transmission should be implemented in populations at risk. (Funded by the Ministry of Science and Technology of China and others.).
casual: Okay, so basically, it looks like this virus was spreading from person to person – like, close contacts were passing it around – starting sometime in mid-December 2019. Because things seem to be moving this way, we’d need to really step up our game and try to slow down the spread if it happens somewhere else too. It’s important for people who are at risk to take steps to stop or cut back on how easily it spreads – you know, like following guidelines. This research was actually funded by the Ministry of Science and Technology of China and a few other groups.

formal: IQ-TREE (http://www.iqtree.org, last accessed February 6, 2020) is a user-friendly and widely used software package for phylogenetic inference using maximum likelihood. Since the release of version 1 in 2014, we have continuously expanded IQ-TREE to integrate a plethora of new models of sequence evolution and efficient computational approaches of phylogenetic inference to deal with genomic data. Here, we describe notable features of IQ-TREE version 2 and highlight the key advantages over other software.
casual: Okay, so IQ-TREE (you can find it at http://www.iqtree.org – I checked it on February 6th, 2020) is a really popular program that people use to figure out how species are related to each other. It’s super easy to use! Since they first released version 1 back in 2014, they've kept adding new stuff – like lots of different ways DNA changes and some clever computer tricks to handle huge amounts of genetic data. Basically, this version 2 is awesome because it's got a bunch of improvements over other programs out there.

formal: Training Deep Neural Networks is complicated by the fact that the distribution of each layer's inputs changes during training, as the parameters of the previous layers change. This slows down the training by requiring lower learning rates and careful parameter initialization, and makes it notoriously hard to train models with saturating nonlinearities. We refer to this phenomenon as internal covariate shift, and address the problem by normalizing layer inputs. Our method draws its strength from making normalization a part of the model architecture and performing the normalization for each training mini-batch. Batch Normalization allows us to use much higher learning rates and be less careful about initialization. It also acts as a regularizer, in some cases eliminating the need for Dropout. Applied to a state-of-the-art image classification model, Batch Normalization achieves the same accuracy with 14 times fewer training steps, and beats the original model by a significant margin. Using an ensemble of batch-normalized networks, we improve upon the best published result on ImageNet classification: reaching 4.9% top-5 validation error (and 4.8% test error), exceeding the accuracy of human raters.
casual:
Okay, so training these super complicated deep neural networks is tricky because things keep changing as they learn. Basically, when one layer adjusts its settings – called parameters – it messes with the information flowing into the layers before it. This makes learning slower; you need to use smaller learning rates and be really careful about how you start things off. It’s also super hard to get these networks working well when they use complicated curves (called nonlinearities) that can get “stuck.” We call this “internal covariate shift,” and what we do is normalize the inputs to each layer.

Our method's good because it makes normalization part of the actual network design, doing it for every small group of data we feed in – we call these "mini-batches." This "Batch Normalization" lets us use much bigger learning rates and not stress so much about how we start things up. Plus, it helps prevent the network from getting stuck on bad patterns, sometimes even letting us ditch Dropout (which is another way to do this). 

We tried it on a really advanced image recognition system, and guess what? It got the same accuracy as before, but took *fourteen* times fewer training steps! And it actually outperformed the original model – by a lot. Even better, when we used a bunch of these batch-normalized networks together (an “ensemble”), we topped even the best results people had ever gotten on ImageNet, hitting 4.9% on the validation set and 4.8% on the test set! That's even better than what human experts could do.

formal: Traffic congestion is one of the growing urban problem with associated problems like fuel wastage, loss of lives, and slow productivity. The existing traffic system uses programming logic control (PLC) with round-robin scheduling algorithm. Recent works have proposed IoT-based frameworks that use traffic density of each lane to control traffic movement, but they suffer from low accuracy due to lack of emergency vehicle image datasets for training deep neural networks. In this paper, we propose a novel distributed IoT framework that is based on two observations. The first observation is major structural changes to road are rare. This observation is exploited by proposing a novel two stage vehicle detector that is able to achieve 77% vehicle detection accuracy on UA-DETRAC dataset. The second observation is emergency vehicle have distinct siren sound that is detected using a novel acoustic detection algorithm on an edge device. The proposed system is able to detect emergency vehicles with an average accuracy of 99.4%.
casual:
Okay, so basically, traffic jams are a huge problem in cities – they waste gas, can be dangerous, and make everyone’s work slower.  Normally, we control traffic using computer programs that just cycle through different routes one after another. Lately, people have been trying to use the internet of things (IoT) to manage traffic by looking at how busy each lane is. But these systems aren't super reliable because they don’t have enough pictures of emergencies to train their AI. 

Here’s what we did instead: We came up with a new, spread-out IoT system based on two key ideas. First, roads don’t really change much – they stay pretty much the same over time.  So, we built a special tool that can spot vehicles really well – it got about 77% right on this dataset called UA-DETRAC. Second, emergency vehicles always make a loud siren! We created a new way to listen for those sirens using a sensor on smaller computers, and it works amazingly well, catching them with almost perfect accuracy – around 99.4%!

formal: In an industrial maintenance context, degradation diagnosis is the problem of determining the current level of degradation of operating machines based on measurements. With the emergence of Machine Learning techniques, such a problem can now be solved by training a degradation model offline and by using it online. While such models are more and more accurate and performant, they are often black-box and their decisions are therefore not interpretable for human maintenance operators. On the contrary, interpretable ML models are able to provide explanations for the model’s decisions and consequently improves the confidence of the human operator about the maintenance decision based on these models. This paper proposes a new method to quantitatively measure the interpretability of such models that is agnostic (no assumption about the class of models) and that is applied on degradation models. The proposed method requires that the decision maker sets up some high level parameters in order to measure the interpretability of the models and then can decide whether the obtained models are satisfactory or not. The method is formally defined and is fully illustrated on a decision tree degradation model and a model trained with a recent neural network architecture called Multiclass Neural Additive Model.
casual:
Okay, so basically, when machines break down in factories, figuring out *how* bad they are – like how much damage has happened – is a big job called “degradation diagnosis.” It’s all about using measurements to see where things stand.

Now, thanks to something called Machine Learning, we can actually do this really well! We can build these models that learn from data and predict how worn out a machine is. You train them once, and then they keep working for you. These models are getting better and better, but often they’re like “black boxes” – meaning no one really understands *why* they make the decisions they do. That makes it hard for maintenance workers to trust them.

That's where interpretable machine learning comes in! If a model can explain itself, it builds more confidence with the person making repairs. This paper is about creating a way to actually measure how understandable these models are – and it doesn’t matter what kind of model it is. It basically asks you to set some key things up, then tells you if the results are good enough for your needs. We show exactly how this works with a simple decision tree model and a more complicated one built using a neural network called Multiclass Neural Additive Model – it's all laid out step-by-step!

formal: April 8, 2009Groups at MIT and NYU have collected a dataset of millions of tiny colour images from the web. It is, in principle, an excellent dataset for unsupervised training of deep generative models, but previous researchers who have tried this have found it di cult to learn a good set of lters from the images. We show how to train a multi-layer generative model that learns to extract meaningful features which resemble those found in the human visual cortex. Using a novel parallelization algorithm to distribute the work among multiple machines connected on a network, we show how training such a model can be done in reasonable time. A second problematic aspect of the tiny images dataset is that there are no reliable class labels which makes it hard to use for object recognition experiments. We created two sets of reliable labels. The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes and the CIFAR-100 set has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes. Using these labels, we show that object recognition is signi cantly
casual:
Okay, so basically, a bunch of researchers at MIT and NYU got their hands on a massive collection of really small color pictures from the internet – like, millions of them! It’s actually super great for teaching computers to create new images without any specific instructions (we call that “unsupervised learning”). But before, people trying to use this data had a *really* hard time getting the computer to learn useful patterns. 

They figured out how to train a complicated model with lots of layers, and it actually started picking up on features in the pictures that are similar to what our brains see – like, the way we recognize things! They did this by splitting the work between several computers connected together, which made the training process much faster. 

The other tricky thing about this dataset is that there weren’t any labels telling you *what* was in each picture (it didn't say "dog" or “cat”). So, they made their own labels! They created two sets: CIFAR-10, which had 6,000 examples of each of ten different things (like cars and trucks), and CIFAR-100, with 600 examples for each of one hundred different categories. Using these new labels, they showed that the computer could actually recognize objects pretty well – it was a big improvement!

formal: This article presents global cancer statistics by world region for the year 2022 based on updated estimates from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). There were close to 20 million new cases of cancer in the year 2022 (including nonmelanoma skin cancers [NMSCs]) alongside 9.7 million deaths from cancer (including NMSC). The estimates suggest that approximately one in five men or women develop cancer in a lifetime, whereas around one in nine men and one in 12 women die from it. Lung cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer in 2022, responsible for almost 2.5 million new cases, or one in eight cancers worldwide (12.4% of all cancers globally), followed by cancers of the female breast (11.6%), colorectum (9.6%), prostate (7.3%), and stomach (4.9%). Lung cancer was also the leading cause of cancer death, with an estimated 1.8 million deaths (18.7%), followed by colorectal (9.3%), liver (7.8%), female breast (6.9%), and stomach (6.8%) cancers. Breast cancer and lung cancer were the most frequent cancers in women and men, respectively (both cases and deaths).
casual:
Okay, so basically, here’s what we know about cancer worldwide from 2022 – and it's pretty serious! The IARC (that’s the International Agency for Research on Cancer) put together these numbers, and they’re based on updated estimates. In 2022, there were almost 20 million new cases of cancer, which includes those non-melanoma skin cancers too – and a staggering 9.7 million people actually died from it, again including the skin cancers.

Looking at it long-term, about one in five men and women will likely get cancer during their lives. That’s roughly one in nine guys and one in twelve gals who will sadly pass away because of it. Lung cancer was *the* most common type – they found almost 2.5 million new cases, which is like one in eight cancers overall (about 12.4%!). Then you had breast cancer at 11.6%, followed by colorectal cancer at 9.6%, prostate cancer at 7.3%, and stomach cancer at 4.9%.

And it wasn’t just diagnosed; lung cancer was also the biggest cause of death, accounting for around 1.8 million deaths (about 18.7%). Colorectal cancer came in second at 9.3%, then liver cancer at 7.8%, breast cancer at 6.9%, and finally stomach cancer at 6.8%. Basically, breast cancer and lung cancer were the biggest problems for women and men, respectively – both when it came to new diagnoses and deaths.

formal: The simultaneous measurement of multiple modalities represents an exciting frontier for single-cell genomics and necessitates computational methods that can define cellular states based on multimodal data. Here, we introduce "weighted-nearest neighbor" analysis, an unsupervised framework to learn the relative utility of each data type in each cell, enabling an integrative analysis of multiple modalities. We apply our procedure to a CITE-seq dataset of 211,000 human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) with panels extending to 228 antibodies to construct a multimodal reference atlas of the circulating immune system. Multimodal analysis substantially improves our ability to resolve cell states, allowing us to identify and validate previously unreported lymphoid subpopulations. Moreover, we demonstrate how to leverage this reference to rapidly map new datasets and to interpret immune responses to vaccination and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Our approach represents a broadly applicable strategy to analyze single-cell multimodal datasets and to look beyond the transcriptome toward a unified and multimodal definition of cellular identity.
casual:
Okay, so this is pretty cool stuff! Basically, when you look at cells using lots of different types of data – like genes *and* protein levels – all at the same time, it opens up a whole new world for understanding what’s going on with single cells. We really needed some smart computer programs to figure out how these different measurements relate to each cell's identity.

That’s where we came in! We created something called “weighted-nearest neighbor” analysis – it’s an automatic way to see which data type (genes or proteins, for example) is most important for describing each individual cell. This lets us put all the different kinds of information together really well. 

We used this on a huge dataset – over 211,000 human blood cells – and looked at 228 different markers to build a detailed map of the immune system in our bodies.  Turns out, looking at everything together helped us spot new types of immune cell populations that we hadn’t seen before!

And here's the best part: we can now use this map super quickly to analyze other datasets too. It’s even helping us understand how people respond to vaccines and to COVID-19.  It’s a really flexible way to study single-cell data, and it helps us move beyond just looking at genes – we can finally create a complete picture of what makes each cell unique!

formal: Each year, the American Cancer Society estimates the numbers of new cancer cases and deaths that will occur in the United States and compiles the most recent data on population-based cancer occurrence. Incidence data (through 2016) were collected by the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program; the National Program of Cancer Registries; and the North American Association of Central Cancer Registries. Mortality data (through 2017) were collected by the National Center for Health Statistics. In 2020, 1,806,590 new cancer cases and 606,520 cancer deaths are projected to occur in the United States. The cancer death rate rose until 1991, then fell continuously through 2017, resulting in an overall decline of 29% that translates into an estimated 2.9 million fewer cancer deaths than would have occurred if peak rates had persisted. This progress is driven by long-term declines in death rates for the 4 leading cancers (lung, colorectal, breast, prostate); however, over the past decade (2008-2017), reductions slowed for female breast and colorectal cancers, and halted for prostate cancer.
casual:
Okay, so basically, every year the American Cancer Society figures out how many new cancer cases are expected and how many deaths they think will happen here in the US. They pull data from a bunch of different sources – like the Surveillance Program, the National Registry, and groups across North America – to get really accurate numbers on where cancer is popping up. Then, for death statistics, they use info from the National Center for Health Statistics. 

As of 2020, they're predicting about 1.8 million new cancer cases and 606,000 deaths. Now, here’s the interesting part: cancer deaths were going up until 1991, but then they started dropping steadily all the way through 2017. This meant a total decrease of around 29%, which is like saying we've avoided about 2.9 million deaths that *would* have happened if things hadn’t gotten better.

The good news is that this drop has been mostly because lung, colorectal, breast, and prostate cancers have seen big declines in death rates over many years. But lately – specifically from 2008 to 2017 – the progress slowed down for breast and colorectal cancer, and it actually stopped completely for prostate cancer.

formal: Emerging infectious diseases, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and Zika virus disease, present a major threat to public health<sup>1-3</sup>. Despite intense research efforts, how, when and where new diseases appear are still a source of considerable uncertainty. A severe respiratory disease was recently reported in Wuhan, Hubei province, China. As of 25 January 2020, at least 1,975 cases had been reported since the first patient was hospitalized on 12 December 2019. Epidemiological investigations have suggested that the outbreak was associated with a seafood market in Wuhan. Here we study a single patient who was a worker at the market and who was admitted to the Central Hospital of Wuhan on 26 December 2019 while experiencing a severe respiratory syndrome that included fever, dizziness and a cough. Metagenomic RNA sequencing<sup>4</sup> of a sample of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid from the patient identified a new RNA virus strain from the family Coronaviridae, which is designated here 'WH-Human 1' coronavirus (and has also been referred to as '2019-nCoV').
casual:
Okay, so basically, things like SARS and Zika are huge problems for public health – they’re really serious! And even though scientists are working super hard on them, we still don’t really know *why* or *where* new diseases pop up. Recently, there was a bad respiratory illness in Wuhan, China. As of January 25th, 2020, over 1,975 people had gotten sick since it started back in December 2019. Scientists think it might have come from a seafood market in that area.

We’re looking at one specific patient – he was a worker at that market and ended up in the hospital on December 26th, 2019, with really bad breathing, fever, dizziness, and a cough. They took some fluid from his lungs (called bronchoalveolar lavage fluid) and did some super-detailed genetic testing called metagenomic RNA sequencing. This found a brand new virus – it’s in the same family as coronaviruses and they've named it 'WH-Human 1' coronavirus, or sometimes just ‘2019-nCoV’.

Okay, so basically, Indonesia has the biggest tropical swampy areas – called peatlands – on Earth, covering about 14.91 million hectares. These peatlands are super important because they help suck up carbon from the atmosphere.

This study was all about figuring out some things in Pesisir Selatan, Sumatra Barat. They wanted to: first, make a map of the peatlands there, second, figure out how much soil carbon was stored in those peatlands depending on what people were doing with the land – like if it was forest or oil palm plantations – and how thick the peat actually was. And third, they looked at how different soil features connected to the amount of carbon.

They collected soil samples from 30 different spots in Pesisir Selatan. The types of land use on those peatlands were mostly forests (called GH), shrubs (GS), oil palm plantations (GPs), annual crops (GLp), and just bare, empty land (also GLp).

Turns out, the whole area covered by peatlands in that region was about 78,998.74 hectares. And they found a massive 244 million tonnes of soil carbon stored there! The order of how much carbon was stored was oil palm plantations first, then shrubs, followed by forests, then grasslands, and lastly the bare land.

The average amount of carbon per hectare was about 3,090.89 – again, oil palms had the most, followed by forests, then grasslands, shrubs, and finally the bare land.  They also looked at how much carbon was stored based on the peat’s depth: around 8,529 tons for really thick peat (over 600cm), 4,082 tons for medium-depth peat (300-600cm), and about 525 tons for thinner peat (0-300cm).

formal: The introduction of AlphaFold 2<sup>1</sup> has spurred a revolution in modelling the structure of proteins and their interactions, enabling a huge range of applications in protein modelling and design<sup>2-6</sup>. Here we describe our AlphaFold 3 model with a substantially updated diffusion-based architecture that is capable of predicting the joint structure of complexes including proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, ions and modified residues. The new AlphaFold model demonstrates substantially improved accuracy over many previous specialized tools: far greater accuracy for protein-ligand interactions compared with state-of-the-art docking tools, much higher accuracy for protein-nucleic acid interactions compared with nucleic-acid-specific predictors and substantially higher antibody-antigen prediction accuracy compared with AlphaFold-Multimer v.2.3<sup>7,8</sup>. Together, these results show that high-accuracy modelling across biomolecular space is possible within a single unified deep-learning framework.
casual: Okay, so basically, this new thing called AlphaFold 2 has totally changed how we figure out what proteins look like and how they work together – it’s opened up tons of possibilities for designing and studying proteins. We've built a new version, AlphaFold 3, which uses a really updated way of thinking that’s based on diffusion. It can actually predict the structure of all sorts of things at once: proteins themselves, DNA, tiny molecules like drugs, ions, and even proteins with special changes to them.  And get this – it's *way* more accurate than most other tools out there! For example, it’s much better than the best computer programs for predicting how a protein interacts with a drug, way more accurate when it comes to figuring out how proteins and DNA connect, and even beats AlphaFold-Multimer v.2.3 in predicting how antibodies and antigens fit together. So, what it all means is that we can now make really precise models of pretty much anything in the biological world using just one super smart computer program!

formal: The Interactive Tree Of Life (https://itol.embl.de) is an online tool for the display, manipulation and annotation of phylogenetic and other trees. It is freely available and open to everyone. iTOL version 5 introduces a completely new tree display engine, together with numerous new features. For example, a new dataset type has been added (MEME motifs), while annotation options have been expanded for several existing ones. Node metadata display options have been extended and now also support non-numerical categorical values, as well as multiple values per node. Direct manual annotation is now available, providing a set of basic drawing and labeling tools, allowing users to draw shapes, labels and other features by hand directly onto the trees. Support for tree and dataset scales has been extended, providing fine control over line and label styles. Unrooted tree displays can now use the equal-daylight algorithm, proving a much greater display clarity. The user account system has been streamlined and expanded with new navigation options and currently handles >1 million trees from >70 000 individual users.
casual:
Okay, so basically, the Interactive Tree of Life (you can find it at https://itol.embl.de) is this super cool online tool where you can look at, change, and add notes to different kinds of family trees – like evolutionary ones! And the best part? It's totally free for anyone to use. 

The newest version, iTOL 5, has a completely rebuilt way of showing off trees, plus lots of new stuff added in. For example, they’ve introduced something called “MEME motifs,” which is a new type of data you can show. Plus, they've made it easier to add notes to some of the existing ones. You can now put different types of information on each branch of the tree, like words or categories, not just numbers! 

You can even draw directly onto the trees yourself – they’ve added tools for drawing shapes and labels by hand. And when it comes to making the trees look nice, you have way more control over things like line styles and label sizes.  It's also been improved so that unrooted trees actually look clearer using a special algorithm. 

Seriously, this thing is amazing! It handles over a million trees created by more than 70,000 people – they’ve even made the system easier to use with new ways to get around and navigate.

formal: Designing complex, dynamic yet multi-functional materials and devices is challenging because the design spaces for these materials have numerous interdependent and often conflicting constraints. Taking inspiration from advances in artificial intelligence and their applications in material discovery, we propose a computational method for designing metamorphic DNA-co-polymerized hydrogel structures. The method consists of a coarse-grained simulation and a deep learning-guided optimization system for exploring the immense design space of these structures. Here, we develop a simple numeric simulation of DNA-co-polymerized hydrogel shape change and seek to find designs for structured hydrogels that can fold into the shapes of different Arabic numerals in different actuation states. We train a convolutional neural network to classify and score the geometric outputs of the coarse-grained simulation to provide autonomous feedback for design optimization. We then construct a genetic algorithm that generates and selects large batches of material designs that compete with one another to evolve and converge on optimal objective-matching designs.
casual:
Okay, so designing really complicated materials and devices – stuff that can change and do lots of things – is super tricky. It’s hard because there are tons of different rules and limitations you have to think about all at once, and they often clash with each other!

We thought, “Hey, what if we looked at how AI finds new materials?” So, we came up with a computer method for making these cool, shape-shifting hydrogels made from DNA and polymers. Basically, it uses two things: a basic computer simulation to see how the hydrogel changes shape, and a smart system that uses deep learning to really fine-tune the designs. 

Our goal is to get these hydrogels to fold themselves into the shapes of Arabic numerals – like 1, 2, 3 – when you push them! We use a simple computer program to simulate how the hydrogel moves. Then, we trained a special AI (a convolutional neural network) to look at what the simulation came up with and give us feedback to help improve the designs automatically.

To really get things moving, we also used something called a genetic algorithm. This system creates tons of different material designs and lets them compete against each other. The best designs – the ones that do what we want—are chosen and then changed slightly over time until they’re super-optimized!

formal: Since the classical molecular dynamics simulator LAMMPS was released as an open source code in 2004, it has become a widely-used tool for particle-based modeling of materials at length scales ranging from atomic to mesoscale to continuum. Reasons for its popularity are that it provides a wide variety of particle interaction models for different materials, that it runs on any platform from a single CPU core to the largest supercomputers with accelerators, and that it gives users control over simulation details, either via the input script or by adding code for new interatomic potentials, constraints, diagnostics, or other features needed for their models. As a result, hundreds of people have contributed new capabilities to LAMMPS and it has grown from fifty thousand lines of code in 2004 to a million lines today. In this paper several of the fundamental algorithms used in LAMMPS are described along with the design strategies which have made it flexible for both users and developers.
casual:
Okay, so basically, LAMMPS – that’s this super popular computer program for simulating how materials work at really small scales – came out back in 2004 as open source, meaning anyone could use it! It’s now used *everywhere* to model things like metals, plastics, and even fluids. You can use it to look at stuff from the tiniest atom level all the way up to how materials behave on a bigger scale.

What makes it so awesome? Well, first, it has tons of different ways to describe how particles interact, so you can use it for almost any material. Second, it runs on pretty much anything – your laptop, huge desktop computers, or even those massive supercomputers that scientists use! And third, you have a *lot* of control over the simulation itself; you can tweak things using a script or even add your own code if you need to. 

Because so many people have been adding new features to it, LAMMPS has grown massively – from just 50,000 lines of code way back when to over a million today! The paper we’re looking at explains the core techniques used in LAMMPS and how they've been designed to be super flexible for both regular users and people building new tools.

formal: We describe "universal" DNA primers for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of a 710-bp fragment of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I gene (COI) from 11 invertebrate phyla: Echinodermata, Mollusca, Annelida, Pogonophora, Arthropoda, Nemertinea, Echiura, Sipuncula, Platyhelminthes, Tardigrada, and Coelenterata, as well as the putative phylum Vestimentifera. Preliminary comparisons revealed that these COI primers generate informative sequences for phylogenetic analyses at the species and higher taxonomic levels.
casual: Okay, so we made some really good DNA primers that work with PCR to make a copy of a specific part of the COI gene – it’s about 710 base pairs long – from a bunch of different invertebrates. We tested them on things like starfish, snails, worms, sponges, insects, ribbon worms, weird fish called echiuros, leeches, flatworms, tardigrades (those super-tough water bears!), and jellyfish. Plus, we even included something called Vestimentifera, which is thought to be its own group. These primers were pretty smart; when we looked at the sequences they made, they gave us enough information to figure out how closely related species are, whether it’s at a basic level or for bigger groups like families and orders.

formal: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), principally ischemic heart disease (IHD) and stroke, are the leading cause of global mortality and a major contributor to disability. This paper reviews the magnitude of total CVD burden, including 13 underlying causes of cardiovascular death and 9 related risk factors, using estimates from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study 2019. GBD, an ongoing multinational collaboration to provide comparable and consistent estimates of population health over time, used all available population-level data sources on incidence, prevalence, case fatality, mortality, and health risks to produce estimates for 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2019. Prevalent cases of total CVD nearly doubled from 271 million (95% uncertainty interval [UI]: 257 to 285 million) in 1990 to 523 million (95% UI: 497 to 550 million) in 2019, and the number of CVD deaths steadily increased from 12.1 million (95% UI:11.4 to 12.6 million) in 1990, reaching 18.6 million (95% UI: 17.1 to 19.7 million) in 2019.
casual:
Okay, so basically, heart problems – like things that cut off blood flow to the heart and strokes – are *the* biggest reason people die worldwide and cause a ton of disability. This report looks at just how big this problem is, checking out nearly 13 different reasons why people die from heart issues and 9 things that make it more likely to happen. It’s all based on data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study 2019.

This GBD study is like a huge project where scientists from all over the world are working together to get really good numbers about how people's health is changing over time. They used tons of information – things like how many new heart problems there were, how common they already were, how often people died from them, and what risks were involved – for almost 200 countries between 1990 and 2019.

Here’s the thing: back in 1990, there were about 271 million people worldwide with heart problems (with a pretty big range of uncertainty). But by 2019, that number had jumped way up to almost 523 million! And sadly, the amount of people dying from those heart issues also went up – from 12.1 million in 1990 to 18.6 million in 2019.

formal: There are a huge number of features which are said to improve Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) accuracy. Practical testing of combinations of such features on large datasets, and theoretical justification of the result, is required. Some features operate on certain models exclusively and for certain problems exclusively, or only for small-scale datasets; while some features, such as batch-normalization and residual-connections, are applicable to the majority of models, tasks, and datasets. We assume that such universal features include Weighted-Residual-Connections (WRC), Cross-Stage-Partial-connections (CSP), Cross mini-Batch Normalization (CmBN), Self-adversarial-training (SAT) and Mish-activation. We use new features: WRC, CSP, CmBN, SAT, Mish activation, Mosaic data augmentation, CmBN, DropBlock regularization, and CIoU loss, and combine some of them to achieve state-of-the-art results: 43.5% AP (65.7% AP50) for the MS COCO dataset at a realtime speed of ~65 FPS on Tesla V100. Source code is at https://github.com/AlexeyAB/darknet
casual:
Okay, so basically, there's tons of stuff people have tried to add to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to make them more accurate. But just saying something *might* help isn’t enough – we need to actually test it out on a lot of data and really understand why it works. 

Some of these improvements only work with certain types of networks or for smaller datasets, you know? Like, things like batch normalization and residual connections are pretty common and can be used in lots of different situations. 

We’re looking at features like Weighted-Residual-Connections (WRC), Cross-Stage-Partial-connections (CSP), something called Cross mini-Batch Normalization (CmBN), Self-adversarial-training (SAT), and the Mish activation function – we think these are pretty universal.  Plus, we threw in Mosaic data augmentation, DropBlock regularization, and CIoU loss to see what happened. 

We ended up mixing some of those together—WRC, CSP, CmBN, SAT, Mish activation, Mosaic, DropBlock, and CIoU loss—and it actually worked really well! We got 43.5% AP (that’s 65.7% AP50) on the MS COCO dataset, and we could do it in real-time at about 65 frames per second using a Tesla V100 GPU. You can find the code over at https://github.com/AlexeyAB/darknet – pretty cool, right?

formal: These 2020 WHO guidelines update previous WHO recommendations released in 2010. They reaffirm messages that some physical activity is better than none, that more physical activity is better for optimal health outcomes and provide a new recommendation on reducing sedentary behaviours. These guidelines highlight the importance of regularly undertaking both aerobic and muscle strengthening activities and for the first time, there are specific recommendations for specific populations including for pregnant and postpartum women and people living with chronic conditions or disability. These guidelines should be used to inform national health policies aligned with the WHO Global Action Plan on Physical Activity 2018-2030 and to strengthen surveillance systems that track progress towards national and global targets.
casual: Okay, so basically, these new WHO guidelines from 2020 are updating older ones made back in 2010. They’re saying the same thing: a little bit of exercise is way better than not exercising at all, and you get even healthier if you do more! They also added a new recommendation about cutting down on sitting around. The guidelines really stress that you should be doing both types of activity – like cardio and strength training – regularly. And here’s the big change: they now have specific advice for different groups of people, including pregnant women, those with postpartum complications, and folks with chronic illnesses or disabilities. It's meant to help countries set their own health policies based on what the WHO wants to achieve by 2030, plus it helps track if we’re actually making progress towards those global goals.

formal: International Nuclear Science, Technology and Engineering Conference 2021 (iNuSTEC2021) “Nuclear Science and Technology for Socio-economic Development” Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM) Skudai, Johor, Malaysia 10-12 October 2021 Editors Nahrul Khair Alang Md Rashid, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Khaidzir Hamzah, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Mohsin Mohd Sies, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Jasman Zainal, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Muhammad Arif Sazali, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Muhammad Syahir Sarkawi, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Nur Syazwani Mohd Ali, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Khairulnadzmi Jamaluddin, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Abdul Aziz Mohamed, Malaysian Nuclear Society Faridah Mohamad Idris, Malaysian Nuclear Agency Julie Andrianny Murshidi, Malaysian Nuclear Agency Faizal K P Kunchi Mohamed, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia Hassan Mohamed, Universiti Tenaga Nasional Abu Hassan Husin, Universiti Teknologi MARA All papers have been peer-reviewed List of Supporting/Sponsoring Organisations, Preface, Contents, iNuSTEC2021 Organising Committee, Inustec 2021 Awards And Recognition, Acknowledgement and Images are available in this pdf
casual:
Okay, so here’s the lowdown on the International Nuclear Science, Technology, and Engineering Conference – iNuSTEC2021. It was all about how nuclear science and tech can help improve economies and communities. Basically, it happened at Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM) in Skudai, Johor, Malaysia from October 10th to 12th, 2021.

The conference was edited by Nahrul Khair Alang Md Rashid, Khaidzir Hamzah, Mohsin Mohd Sies, Jasman Zainal, Muhammad Arif Sazali, Muhammad Syahir Sarkawi, Nur Syazwani Mohd Ali, Khairulnadzmi Jamaluddin, and Abdul Aziz Mohamed – all from UTM. Plus, they had help from folks at the Malaysian Nuclear Society and the Malaysian Nuclear Agency, like Julie Andrianny Murshidi and Faizal K P Kunchi Mohamed (from the Nuclear Agency).  And even someone from Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, Hassan Mohamed, plus people from Tenaga Nasional (Abu Hassan Husin) and Universiti Teknologi MARA (All).

Every single paper presented at the conference went through a really thorough review process – they were all peer-reviewed. You'll also find a list of supporting organizations, a preface, the table of contents, details about the organizing committee, information on the awards, an acknowledgment section, and images – everything’s packed into one PDF!

formal: Excess energy intake can trigger an uncontrolled inﬂammatory response, leading to systemic low-grade inﬂammation and metabolic disturbances that are hypothesised to contribute to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. The long chain n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC n-3 PUFAs) eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) are suggested to mitigate this inﬂammatoryresponse,butthemechanismsareunclear,especiallyatthetissuelevel. Adiposetissues, the ﬁrst tissues to give an inﬂammatory response, may be an important target site of action for EPA and DHA. To evaluate the eﬀects of EPA and DHA in white and brown adipose tissues, we fed male C57Bl/6J mice either a high fat diet (HFD) with 5% corn oil, an HFD with 40% of the corn oil substituted for puriﬁed EPA and DHA triglycerides (HFD-ED), or normal chow, for 8 weeks. Fatty acid proﬁling and transcriptomics were used to study how EPA and DHA aﬀect retroperitoneal whiteandbrownadiposetissues. HFD-EDfedmiceshowedreducedlipidaccumulationandlevelsof the pro-inﬂammatory fatty acid arachidonic acid in both white and brown adipose tissues, compared withHFD-cornoilfedanimals.
casual:
Okay, so basically, when we eat way too many calories, it can actually cause our bodies to start fighting itself off constantly – like a never-ending inflammation. This constant low-level inflammation is thought to be a big reason why heart problems and type 2 diabetes develop.

Now, there are these special fats called long chain n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, specifically EPA and DHA, that scientists think might help calm things down. But honestly, we don’t really know *how* they work, especially when it comes to exactly what's happening inside our bodies. 

It looks like fat tissue is the first place where this inflammation starts, so maybe those EPA and DHA could be really effective there. We did an experiment with mice – basically, we fed some a super fatty diet, some the same diet but with added EPA and DHA, and some normal food for eight weeks. Then we looked at their white and brown fat tissue to see what was going on.

The mice that got the EPA and DHA (HFD-ED) had less fat building up in their fat cells, and they also had way fewer of those bad inflammatory fats called arachidonic acid – both in their white and brown fat. This was compared to the mice who just ate the regular fatty diet.

formal: BACKGROUND: Since December 2019, when coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) emerged in Wuhan city and rapidly spread throughout China, data have been needed on the clinical characteristics of the affected patients. METHODS: We extracted data regarding 1099 patients with laboratory-confirmed Covid-19 from 552 hospitals in 30 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities in mainland China through January 29, 2020. The primary composite end point was admission to an intensive care unit (ICU), the use of mechanical ventilation, or death. RESULTS: The median age of the patients was 47 years; 41.9% of the patients were female. The primary composite end point occurred in 67 patients (6.1%), including 5.0% who were admitted to the ICU, 2.3% who underwent invasive mechanical ventilation, and 1.4% who died. Only 1.9% of the patients had a history of direct contact with wildlife. Among nonresidents of Wuhan, 72.3% had contact with residents of Wuhan, including 31.3% who had visited the city. The most common symptoms were fever (43.8% on admission and 88.7% during hospitalization) and cough (67.8%). Diarrhea was uncommon (3.8%).
casual:
Okay, so basically, back in December 2019, this thing called Covid-19 started popping up in Wuhan, China, and it spread super fast. We really needed to know what was going on with people who got sick.

What we did was gather info from over a thousand patients – exactly 1,099 – who had been officially diagnosed with Covid-19. These patients came from hospitals all across China—we’re talking about 552 hospitals in 30 different places. We collected this data up until January 29th, 2020.

The main thing we were looking at was whether people ended up needing serious care – like going to the ICU, needing a breathing machine, or sadly, dying.

And here's what we found: The average age of those patients was around 47, and about 42% of them were women. About 67 people (that’s roughly 6%) had this bad outcome – they either went to the ICU, needed a ventilator, or passed away. A little over 5% ended up needing help breathing in an intensive care unit, just under 3% needed a full-blown breathing machine, and about 1.4% sadly died.

It's interesting too—only about 2% of these patients had been in contact with wild animals. Most of the people (72%) hadn’t grown up in Wuhan, but many of them *had* spent time there; around 31% even visited the city! The most common symptoms were fever (most people got it when they first showed up and again while they were sick) and a cough—about 68% of people had those.  Diarrhea was pretty rare, only showing up in about 4%.

formal: Generative adversarial networks are a kind of artificial intelligence algorithm designed to solve the generative modeling problem. The goal of a generative model is to study a collection of training examples and learn the probability distribution that generated them. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are then able to generate more examples from the estimated probability distribution. Generative models based on deep learning are common, but GANs are among the most successful generative models (especially in terms of their ability to generate realistic high-resolution images). GANs have been successfully applied to a wide variety of tasks (mostly in research settings) but continue to present unique challenges and research opportunities because they are based on game theory while most other approaches to generative modeling are based on optimization.
casual:
Okay, so basically, Generative Adversarial Networks – or GANs – are a type of AI that’s really good at making things up! They're built to tackle this thing called “generative modeling.” Basically, you give them lots of examples—like tons of pictures—and they try to figure out how those examples were made. It’s like learning the rules behind a collection of drawings. Then, they can actually create *new* examples that look similar, based on what they learned. 

Deep learning generative models are pretty common, but GANs have been super successful, especially when it comes to making really realistic, detailed images. They've been used for all sorts of things – mostly in research labs right now – and they still pose some tricky problems. That’s because they use a bit of game theory, which is different from how most other generative models work; they’re built around competing against each other!

formal: In patients hospitalized with Covid-19, the use of dexamethasone resulted in lower 28-day mortality among those who were receiving either invasive mechanical ventilation or oxygen alone at randomization but not among those receiving no respiratory support. (Funded by the Medical Research Council and National Institute for Health Research and others; RECOVERY ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04381936; ISRCTN number, 50189673.).
casual: Okay, so basically, when doctors gave patients with COVID-19 who were in the hospital dexamethasone – a steroid medicine – it helped lower their chances of dying within 28 days. But this was *only* true for people who were already needing help breathing, like on a ventilator or just using oxygen when they got to the hospital. It didn't seem to make much difference for folks who weren’t getting any extra respiratory support. This research was funded by several groups, including the Medical Research Council and the National Institute for Health Research, and you can find all the details about it in ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04381936) or ISRCTN (50189673).

formal: The study of extracellular vesicles (EVs) has the potential to identify unknown cellular and molecular mechanisms in intercellular communication and in organ homeostasis and disease. Exosomes, with an average diameter of ~100 nanometers, are a subset of EVs. The biogenesis of exosomes involves their origin in endosomes, and subsequent interactions with other intracellular vesicles and organelles generate the final content of the exosomes. Their diverse constituents include nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, amino acids, and metabolites, which can reflect their cell of origin. In various diseases, exosomes offer a window into altered cellular or tissue states, and their detection in biological fluids potentially offers a multicomponent diagnostic readout. The efficient exchange of cellular components through exosomes can inform their applied use in designing exosome-based therapeutics.
casual: Okay, so basically, looking at tiny packages called extracellular vesicles – we call them EVs – is really interesting because it could help us figure out how cells talk to each other and keep our bodies running smoothly, especially when things go wrong like with diseases.  These EVs come in different types; exosomes are the smallest ones, about 100 nanometers across. They’re made when little bubbles called endosomes get involved, then they team up with other parts of the cell to build what's inside. These exosomes are packed with all sorts of stuff – DNA, proteins, fats, amino acids, even tiny chemicals – and it can actually tell you which cell created them!  Because of this, they’re a great way to see what’s happening in cells when there’s a disease. And, cool thing, we can find them in things like blood, so it could be used for really detailed tests. Plus, since exosomes carry stuff between cells, scientists are even trying to use them to create new medicines!

formal: The PRISMA 2020 statement includes a checklist of 27 items to guide reporting of systematic reviews In this article we explain why reporting of each item is recommended, present bullet points that detail the reporting recommendations, and present examples from published reviews We hope that uptake of the PRISMA 2020 statement will lead to more transparent, complete, and accurate reporting of systematic reviews, thus facilitating evidence based decision making on 1 September
casual: Okay, so basically, there's this thing called PRISMA 2020 – it’s like a really helpful checklist with 27 steps that guides how we write reports about systematic reviews. This article is going to break down why following each step is important. We’ll list out the recommendations in simple bullet points and even show you examples from actual published reviews. The whole point is to make sure systematic review reports are super clear, really thorough, and accurate, which will then help people use the evidence properly when making decisions – all starting on September 1st!

formal: To the colonized, the term 'research' is conflated with European colonialism; the ways in which academic research has been implicated in the throes of imperialism remains a painful memory. This essential volume explores intersections of imperialism and research - specifically, the ways in which imperialism is embedded in disciplines of knowledge and tradition as 'regimes of truth.' Concepts such as 'discovery' and 'claiming' are discussed and an argument presented that the decolonization of research methods will help to reclaim control over indigenous ways of knowing and being.Now in its eagerly awaited second edition, this bestselling book has been substantially revised, with new case-studies and examples and important additions on new indigenous literature, the role of research in indigenous struggles for social justice, which brings this essential volume urgently up-to-date. Quelle: Klappentext.
casual:
Okay, so basically, for people who were colonized, the word “research” still carries a lot of baggage because it’s linked to all the bad stuff that colonialism did. It’s a really painful reminder of how research was used to support empires back then. This book dives into exactly where imperialism and research overlap – like how those ideas about research are actually built on old, imperial power structures. They call these structures “regimes of truth,” which basically means they decide what's considered real. The book looks at things like "discovery" and even "claiming” land, and it makes a strong argument that getting rid of colonial ways of doing research can help indigenous communities take control of their own traditions and knowledge. 

And guess what? This is the second edition of a super popular book, so they’ve totally updated it! It has new examples and case studies, plus some important additions about how research plays a role in indigenous people fighting for social justice – which makes it really relevant today.

formal: The outbreak of a novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV) represents a pandemic threat that has been declared a public health emergency of international concern. The CoV spike (S) glycoprotein is a key target for vaccines, therapeutic antibodies, and diagnostics. To facilitate medical countermeasure development, we determined a 3.5-angstrom-resolution cryo-electron microscopy structure of the 2019-nCoV S trimer in the prefusion conformation. The predominant state of the trimer has one of the three receptor-binding domains (RBDs) rotated up in a receptor-accessible conformation. We also provide biophysical and structural evidence that the 2019-nCoV S protein binds angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) with higher affinity than does severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS)-CoV S. Additionally, we tested several published SARS-CoV RBD-specific monoclonal antibodies and found that they do not have appreciable binding to 2019-nCoV S, suggesting that antibody cross-reactivity may be limited between the two RBDs. The structure of 2019-nCoV S should enable the rapid development and evaluation of medical countermeasures to address the ongoing public health crisis.
casual: Okay, so basically, this new coronavirus – called 2019-nCov – is a really big deal and has been labeled a global health emergency. Scientists are focusing on something called the “spike” protein (S) from the virus because it’s super important for making vaccines, medicines, and tests. They actually figured out a detailed 3D structure of this spike protein using super-powerful microscopes – like, it was resolved at 3.5 angstroms! This structure shows that one of the parts of the protein that grabs onto cells (called the receptor-binding domain or RBD) is sticking up and exposed, which is key. Plus, they found out that this new coronavirus’s spike protein actually attaches to a different enzyme called ACE2 with more strength than the similar protein from the SARS virus. They also checked out some existing antibody tests against the SARS virus and discovered that most of them didn't stick to the 2019-nCov spike protein – meaning there isn’t much overlap in how these antibodies recognize the two proteins. This new structure is going to help scientists quickly develop treatments and ways to fight this pandemic, which is awesome!

formal: UCSF ChimeraX is the next-generation interactive visualization program from the Resource for Biocomputing, Visualization, and Informatics (RBVI), following UCSF Chimera. ChimeraX brings (a) significant performance and graphics enhancements; (b) new implementations of Chimera's most highly used tools, many with further improvements; (c) several entirely new analysis features; (d) support for new areas such as virtual reality, light-sheet microscopy, and medical imaging data; (e) major ease-of-use advances, including toolbars with icons to perform actions with a single click, basic "undo" capabilities, and more logical and consistent commands; and (f) an app store for researchers to contribute new tools. ChimeraX includes full user documentation and is free for noncommercial use, with downloads available for Windows, Linux, and macOS from https://www.rbvi.ucsf.edu/chimerax.
casual: Okay, so basically, UCSF ChimeraX is the super-updated version of a really popular computer program called Chimera – it’s made by the RBVI group. It's got some huge improvements! First off, it’s way faster and looks much better thanks to all the new graphics. They’ve also taken the tools people used most in the original Chimera and made them even better. Plus, they added tons of totally new ways to analyze stuff. Seriously, it now supports things like virtual reality, light-sheet microscopy, and even medical imaging data. And get this – it's way easier to use! They’ve added toolbars with icons so you can do things with just one click, plus a simple “undo” feature and commands that actually make sense. There’s also an app store where researchers can share their own tools. You can find the full documentation and download it for free (for non-commercial use) on their website: https://www.rbvi.ucsf.edu/chimerax. It works on Windows, Linux, and macOS!

formal: ColabFold offers accelerated prediction of protein structures and complexes by combining the fast homology search of MMseqs2 with AlphaFold2 or RoseTTAFold. ColabFold's 40-60-fold faster search and optimized model utilization enables prediction of close to 1,000 structures per day on a server with one graphics processing unit. Coupled with Google Colaboratory, ColabFold becomes a free and accessible platform for protein folding. ColabFold is open-source software available at https://github.com/sokrypton/ColabFold and its novel environmental databases are available at https://colabfold.mmseqs.com .
casual: Okay, so basically, ColabFold is a super cool tool that lets you figure out protein structures really quickly! It does this by teaming up the speedy searching of MMseqs2 with either AlphaFold2 or RoseTTAFold – both are awesome programs for predicting shapes.  It’s like 40 to 60 times faster than normal, which means it can predict almost a thousand protein structures each day using just one graphics card! Plus, because it works with Google Colab, you can use it totally free and everyone can access it. You can find the software itself on GitHub at https://github.com/sokrypton/ColabFold, and there’s also a website – https://colabfold.mmseqs.com – where you can find these new environmental databases they're using!

formal: Deep learning has revolutionized many machine learning tasks in recent years, ranging from image classification and video processing to speech recognition and natural language understanding. The data in these tasks are typically represented in the Euclidean space. However, there is an increasing number of applications, where data are generated from non-Euclidean domains and are represented as graphs with complex relationships and interdependency between objects. The complexity of graph data has imposed significant challenges on the existing machine learning algorithms. Recently, many studies on extending deep learning approaches for graph data have emerged. In this article, we provide a comprehensive overview of graph neural networks (GNNs) in data mining and machine learning fields. We propose a new taxonomy to divide the state-of-the-art GNNs into four categories, namely, recurrent GNNs, convolutional GNNs, graph autoencoders, and spatial-temporal GNNs.
