We further discuss the applications of GNNs across various domains and summarize the open-source codes, benchmark data sets, and model evaluation of GNNs.
casual:
Okay, so basically, deep learning has totally changed a ton of things in machine learning – like figuring out what’s in pictures, understanding videos, recognizing voices, and even making sense of language. Usually, all this works with numbers that live in straight lines, called Euclidean space. But now, there are way more jobs where the data is super complicated—think of it like networks or webs of stuff, where everything's linked together and depends on each other. This “graph” data makes it really hard for regular machine learning programs to work properly. Lately, lots of people have been trying to adapt deep learning to handle this kind of graph data.

This article gives you a breakdown of something called Graph Neural Networks, or GNNs – they’re becoming super important in things like data mining and just general machine learning. We've come up with a new way to group all the different types of GNNs out there, breaking them down into four main groups: recurrent ones, convolutional ones, graph autoencoders, and even those that deal with space and time. Plus, we talk about how these GNNs are being used in different fields and point you towards some helpful open-source code, datasets, and ways to measure how well they’re doing!

formal: Older age was associated with greater risk of development of ARDS and death likely owing to less rigorous immune response. Although high fever was associated with the development of ARDS, it was also associated with better outcomes among patients with ARDS. Moreover, treatment with methylprednisolone may be beneficial for patients who develop ARDS.
casual: Okay, so basically, getting older when someone got really sick and developed ARDS – that’s linked to a much higher chance of things going badly and sadly, dying. It seems like their immune system wasn't working as strongly as it should have been. Now, high fevers actually seemed to help some people with ARDS; weirdly enough, they did better! And, researchers think giving them methylprednisolone might also be a good idea if they get ARDS.

formal: The hallmarks of cancer conceptualization is a heuristic tool for distilling the vast complexity of cancer phenotypes and genotypes into a provisional set of underlying principles. As knowledge of cancer mechanisms has progressed, other facets of the disease have emerged as potential refinements. Herein, the prospect is raised that phenotypic plasticity and disrupted differentiation is a discrete hallmark capability, and that nonmutational epigenetic reprogramming and polymorphic microbiomes both constitute distinctive enabling characteristics that facilitate the acquisition of hallmark capabilities. Additionally, senescent cells, of varying origins, may be added to the roster of functionally important cell types in the tumor microenvironment. SIGNIFICANCE: Cancer is daunting in the breadth and scope of its diversity, spanning genetics, cell and tissue biology, pathology, and response to therapy. Ever more powerful experimental and computational tools and technologies are providing an avalanche of "big data" about the myriad manifestations of the diseases that cancer encompasses.
casual: Okay, so basically, the idea of “hallmarks of cancer” is like a shortcut—it helps us make sense of all the crazy different ways cancer can show up, both in how it looks and what’s going on with its genes. As scientists have learned more about cancer, we've realized there are even more important things to consider. It seems like “phenotypic plasticity” (basically, being really adaptable) and messed-up cell development are a key part of how cancer works. Plus, it turns out that changes in our DNA *without* actually changing the genes themselves—called epigenetic reprogramming—and having different types of bacteria in our bodies (our microbiomes) are also super important for allowing cancer to do all this stuff. And finally, older cells that don't divide anymore – called senescent cells – play a role too, especially inside the tumor itself. Seriously, cancer is so complicated because it involves everything from genes and cells to how doctors treat it, and we’re getting tons of information thanks to new technology!

formal: Cellular life depends on a complex web of functional associations between biomolecules. Among these associations, protein-protein interactions are particularly important due to their versatility, specificity and adaptability. The STRING database aims to integrate all known and predicted associations between proteins, including both physical interactions as well as functional associations. To achieve this, STRING collects and scores evidence from a number of sources: (i) automated text mining of the scientific literature, (ii) databases of interaction experiments and annotated complexes/pathways, (iii) computational interaction predictions from co-expression and from conserved genomic context and (iv) systematic transfers of interaction evidence from one organism to another. STRING aims for wide coverage; the upcoming version 11.5 of the resource will contain more than 14 000 organisms. In this update paper, we describe changes to the text-mining system, a new scoring-mode for physical interactions, as well as extensive user interface features for customizing, extending and sharing protein networks.
casual:
Okay, so basically, all living things rely on these super complicated relationships between tiny molecules – like proteins working together. Protein connections are especially key because they can do so many different jobs, and they’re really good at it! The STRING database is trying to map out *every* known connection between proteins, including both when proteins actually touch each other and how they work together. 

They do this by gathering info from a bunch of places: first, they automatically search through tons of scientific papers; second, they use databases that show experiments and groups of proteins working together; third, they guess about connections based on how much proteins are expressed and their DNA – it’s like predicting relationships; and fourth, they move connection data between different animals and plants. STRING wants to cover as many organisms as possible—the next version (11.5) will have over 14,000!  And in this paper, we're talking about updates to their system for searching papers, a new way to rate physical connections, plus lots of new tools that let users change, add to, and share protein networks.

formal: A large body of literature is available on wound healing in humans. Nonetheless, a standardized ex vivo wound model without disruption of the dermal compartment has not been put forward with compelling justification. Here, we present a novel wound model based on application of negative pressure and its effects for epidermal regeneration and immune cell behaviour. Importantly, the basement membrane remained intact after blister roof removal and keratinocytes were absent in the wounded area. Upon six days of culture, the wound was covered with one to three-cell thick K14<sup>+</sup>Ki67<sup>+</sup> keratinocyte layers, indicating that proliferation and migration were involved in wound closure. After eight to twelve days, a multi-layered epidermis was formed expressing epidermal differentiation markers (K10, filaggrin, DSG-1, CDSN). Investigations about immune cell-specific manners revealed more T cells in the blister roof epidermis compared to normal epidermis.
casual: Okay, so there’s tons of research on how our skin heals – it’s a really big topic! But honestly, we haven't had a really good way to test this stuff outside the body that doesn’t mess up the bottom layer of skin. That’s why we created a new model using suction and looked at how quickly the top layers of skin grew back and how our immune cells reacted. The cool thing is, when we took off the blisters, the basement membrane – you know, the strong support structure – stayed perfectly intact, and there were no dead skin cells (keratinocytes) in the wound itself. After about six days in a lab dish, the wound was covered with layers of these special skin cells called K14+Ki67+ – that meant they were actively growing and moving around to close it up! Then, over eight to twelve days, we saw fully formed, multi-layered skin with all the usual markers for healthy skin (like K10, filaggrin, DSG-1, CDSN). We also noticed something interesting: there were more T cells in the blister tissue compared to normal skin – which tells us about how the immune system is involved.

formal: Functional enrichment analysis is pivotal for interpreting high-throughput omics data in life science. It is crucial for this type of tool to use the latest annotation databases for as many organisms as possible. To meet these requirements, we present here an updated version of our popular Bioconductor package, clusterProfiler 4.0. This package has been enhanced considerably compared with its original version published 9 years ago. The new version provides a universal interface for functional enrichment analysis in thousands of organisms based on internally supported ontologies and pathways as well as annotation data provided by users or derived from online databases. It also extends the dplyr and ggplot2 packages to offer tidy interfaces for data operation and visualization. Other new features include gene set enrichment analysis and comparison of enrichment results from multiple gene lists. We anticipate that clusterProfiler 4.0 will be applied to a wide range of scenarios across diverse organisms.
casual: Okay, so basically, functional enrichment analysis is super important when you’re looking at all those massive amounts of data from things like genomics – it really helps scientists figure out what’s going on in biology! To do this well, you absolutely need the most up-to-date information about different creatures, and we've made a big update to our tool, clusterProfiler 4.0. It’s way improved compared to the original version, which was released almost ten years ago! Now, it lets you analyze what functions are being affected by your data across thousands of organisms – using its own lists of pathways and categories, plus any info *you* add or get from other online databases. Plus, we've added some cool extras like making things easier to work with using the dplyr and ggplot2 packages for handling and showing off your data. We’ve also included gene set enrichment analysis and a way to compare results when you have multiple lists of genes you're looking at. We think clusterProfiler 4.0 will be used in all sorts of different situations with many different kinds of organisms!

formal: Much of the complexity within cells arises from functional and regulatory interactions among proteins. The core of these interactions is increasingly known, but novel interactions continue to be discovered, and the information remains scattered across different database resources, experimental modalities and levels of mechanistic detail. The STRING database (https://string-db.org/) systematically collects and integrates protein-protein interactions-both physical interactions as well as functional associations. The data originate from a number of sources: automated text mining of the scientific literature, computational interaction predictions from co-expression, conserved genomic context, databases of interaction experiments and known complexes/pathways from curated sources. All of these interactions are critically assessed, scored, and subsequently automatically transferred to less well-studied organisms using hierarchical orthology information. The data can be accessed via the website, but also programmatically and via bulk downloads.
casual:
Okay, so basically, a lot of what makes cells work is all about how different proteins talk to each other and control things. We’re starting to really understand these connections, but there are still tons of new ones being found – and the info's spread out everywhere! There’s this amazing database called STRING (you can find it at https://string-db.org/) that does a really good job of bringing everything together. It tracks all sorts of protein interactions – like how they physically stick together, but also what they do with each other functionally. 

The data comes from lots of places: scientists have basically read tons of research papers and pulled out the important bits, predicted connections based on how proteins are expressed, looked at their DNA to see if they’re similar, used results from actual experiments where they tested interactions, and even taken in information about known complexes and pathways that experts have already put together. Seriously, everything's been carefully checked and scored! Then, the database uses clever info about related organisms – called orthology – to automatically copy this data over to less-studied creatures too. You can check it out on their website, or even get the data by computer program or downloading a big file if you need it.

formal: BACKGROUND: Coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) is associated with diffuse lung damage. Glucocorticoids may modulate inflammation-mediated lung injury and thereby reduce progression to respiratory failure and death. METHODS: In this controlled, open-label trial comparing a range of possible treatments in patients who were hospitalized with Covid-19, we randomly assigned patients to receive oral or intravenous dexamethasone (at a dose of 6 mg once daily) for up to 10 days or to receive usual care alone. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Here, we report the final results of this assessment. RESULTS: A total of 2104 patients were assigned to receive dexamethasone and 4321 to receive usual care. Overall, 482 patients (22.9%) in the dexamethasone group and 1110 patients (25.7%) in the usual care group died within 28 days after randomization (age-adjusted rate ratio, 0.83; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.75 to 0.93; P<0.001). The proportional and absolute between-group differences in mortality varied considerably according to the level of respiratory support that the patients were receiving at the time of randomization.
casual:
Okay, so basically, Covid-19 really messes up your lungs – it causes damage all over. Now, doctors found that steroid medicine called dexamethasone could actually help a lot. It seems like these steroids can cut down on the inflammation in your lungs and stop the disease from getting way worse, which could then prevent you from needing breathing machines or even dying.

Here's how we looked at it: We did a study with over 6,000 hospitalized patients who had Covid-19. We randomly split them into two groups – one group got dexamethasone (6mg once a day for up to 10 days, either by mouth or IV) and the other group just got their regular care. The main thing we were watching for was how many people died within 28 days of starting treatment.

Turns out, only 22.9% of the people who took dexamethasone died (that’s 482 people out of 2104), compared to 25.7% of those who just got regular care (which was 1110 people out of 4321). And that difference in death rates was really significant – it was about 83% (0.83) less likely for the dexamethasone group to die, with a pretty strong confidence level (95% certainty!).

But here's the tricky part: how much support each person needed – like if they were on oxygen or breathing machines – made a big difference in how well the steroid worked.

formal: Abstract The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (AlphaFold DB, https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) is an openly accessible, extensive database of high-accuracy protein-structure predictions. Powered by AlphaFold v2.0 of DeepMind, it has enabled an unprecedented expansion of the structural coverage of the known protein-sequence space. AlphaFold DB provides programmatic access to and interactive visualization of predicted atomic coordinates, per-residue and pairwise model-confidence estimates and predicted aligned errors. The initial release of AlphaFold DB contains over 360,000 predicted structures across 21 model-organism proteomes, which will soon be expanded to cover most of the (over 100 million) representative sequences from the UniRef90 data set.
casual:
Okay, so basically, this thing called AlphaFold DB – you can find it at https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk – is a massive database of predicted protein structures. It’s super cool because it uses something called AlphaFold v2.0 from DeepMind, and it's really accurate! This has totally opened up our understanding of how proteins are shaped. 

Basically, the DB lets you get access to these predictions programmatically – meaning through code – and also gives you tools to see them visually. It even tells you how confident AlphaFold is in each prediction and shows you where the errors might be. The first version has over 360,000 predicted structures for 21 different sets of proteins (from 21 different organisms), and they're planning on expanding it to include almost 100 million protein sequences from a huge database called UniRef90!

formal: Understanding global communications among cells requires accurate representation of cell-cell signaling links and effective systems-level analyses of those links. We construct a database of interactions among ligands, receptors and their cofactors that accurately represent known heteromeric molecular complexes. We then develop CellChat, a tool that is able to quantitatively infer and analyze intercellular communication networks from single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. CellChat predicts major signaling inputs and outputs for cells and how those cells and signals coordinate for functions using network analysis and pattern recognition approaches. Through manifold learning and quantitative contrasts, CellChat classifies signaling pathways and delineates conserved and context-specific pathways across different datasets. Applying CellChat to mouse and human skin datasets shows its ability to extract complex signaling patterns. Our versatile and easy-to-use toolkit CellChat and a web-based Explorer ( http://www.cellchat.org/ ) will help discover novel intercellular communications and build cell-cell communication atlases in diverse tissues.
casual:
Okay, so basically, figuring out how cells talk to each other across the body is tricky – we need to really understand which cells are sending signals to which others and how those connections work together. We’ve built a big database that lists all the different molecules involved in cell-to-cell communication, like the things that trigger responses and the helpers they use. 

Then, we created CellChat, which is a tool that can actually figure out these communication networks from single-cell data – specifically, when we look at what genes are turned on or off in individual cells. It’s smart because it uses computer analysis to predict which signals are coming into and going out of cells, and how they all work together to do things. 

CellChat even uses techniques like looking at the “shape” of data to group similar pathways and spot patterns that stick around across different tissues – we used this on skin samples from mice and humans, and it was really good at finding complicated signaling connections.  Ultimately, CellChat is a super helpful toolkit (and has a website: http://www.cellchat.org/) that will help scientists discover new ways cells communicate and even build complete maps of cell-to-cell communication in different parts of the body!

formal: Thomas Wolf, Lysandre Debut, Victor Sanh, Julien Chaumond, Clement Delangue, Anthony Moi, Pierric Cistac, Tim Rault, Remi Louf, Morgan Funtowicz, Joe Davison, Sam Shleifer, Patrick von Platen, Clara Ma, Yacine Jernite, Julien Plu, Canwen Xu, Teven Le Scao, Sylvain Gugger, Mariama Drame, Quentin Lhoest, Alexander Rush. Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations. 2020.
casual: Okay, so basically this is a collection of papers—like, really detailed reports—from the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. It’s called “System Demonstrations,” which means they're showing off how different computer programs actually *work* and what they can do with language. The paper was put out in 2020, and it includes work from a bunch of smart folks: Thomas Wolf, Lysandre Debut, Victor Sanh, Julien Chaumond, Clement Delangue, Anthony Moi, Pierric Cistac, Tim Rault, Remi Louf, Morgan Funtowicz, Joe Davison, Sam Shleifer, Patrick von Platen, Clara Ma, Yacine Jernite, Julien Plu, Canwen Xu, Teven Le Scao, Sylvain Gugger, Mariama Drame, Quentin Lhoest, and Alexander Rush. Pretty cool, right?

formal: The World Health Organization (WHO) on March 11, 2020, has declared the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) outbreak a global pandemic (1). At a news briefing , WHO Director-General, Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, noted that over the past 2 weeks, the number of cases outside China increased 13-fold and the number of countries with cases increased threefold. Further increases are expected. He said that the WHO is "deeply concerned both by the alarming levels of spread and severity and by the alarming levels of inaction," and he called on countries to take action now to contain the virus. "We should double down," he said. "We should be more aggressive." [...].
casual: Okay, so basically, back in March 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) officially declared that COVID-19 – this new coronavirus – was a worldwide pandemic (1). It’s like, they realized it wasn't just one problem anymore. The WHO head guy, Dr. Tedros, said things were getting seriously bad really fast. Over the last couple of weeks, cases outside of China had jumped a huge 13 times, and the number of countries reporting infections had tripled! He thinks it’s going to keep getting worse. He was super worried about how quickly it was spreading and how badly people were getting sick – and he was also really frustrated that not enough people were actually doing anything to stop it. He urged all the countries to step up their game and be more proactive, saying they needed to “double down” and get even more aggressive with containment efforts.

formal: The present outbreak of a coronavirus-associated acute respiratory disease called coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19) is the third documented spillover of an animal coronavirus to humans in only two decades that has resulted in a major epidemic. The Coronaviridae Study Group (CSG) of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses, which is responsible for developing the classification of viruses and taxon nomenclature of the family Coronaviridae, has assessed the placement of the human pathogen, tentatively named 2019-nCoV, within the Coronaviridae. Based on phylogeny, taxonomy and established practice, the CSG recognizes this virus as forming a sister clade to the prototype human and bat severe acute respiratory syndrome coronaviruses (SARS-CoVs) of the species Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus, and designates it as SARS-CoV-2. In order to facilitate communication, the CSG proposes to use the following naming convention for individual isolates: SARS-CoV-2/host/location/isolate/date.
casual:
Okay, so basically, this whole COVID-19 thing – that’s a really serious illness caused by a coronavirus – is actually the third time we've seen a virus jump from animals to humans in just two decades, and it’s created a huge worldwide problem. Scientists have been looking closely at how this new virus fits into the family of coronaviruses, and they’re part of a group called the CSG that sorts out how viruses are classified.  

They've figured out that this virus, which was initially called 2019-nCoV, is super close to other human and bat coronaviruses like those that caused SARS – it's basically a sibling! They’re officially calling it SARS-CoV-2. To make sure everyone understands things, the scientists are using a specific naming system:  SARS-CoV-2/where it came from/where they found it/the exact version/when they got it.

formal: The Pfam database is a widely used resource for classifying protein sequences into families and domains. Since Pfam was last described in this journal, over 350 new families have been added in Pfam 33.1 and numerous improvements have been made to existing entries. To facilitate research on COVID-19, we have revised the Pfam entries that cover the SARS-CoV-2 proteome, and built new entries for regions that were not covered by Pfam. We have reintroduced Pfam-B which provides an automatically generated supplement to Pfam and contains 136 730 novel clusters of sequences that are not yet matched by a Pfam family. The new Pfam-B is based on a clustering by the MMseqs2 software. We have compared all of the regions in the RepeatsDB to those in Pfam and have started to use the results to build and refine Pfam repeat families. Pfam is freely available for browsing and download at http://pfam.xfam.org/.
casual:
Okay, so basically, the Pfam database is super popular – it’s like a giant guidebook that helps scientists figure out which groups proteins belong to. It's been updated loads since the last time this was written in the journal! They added over 350 new protein families in version 33.1, and they also made tons of improvements to the existing entries too.

To help with research on COVID-19, they’ve really focused on the proteins from SARS-CoV-2 – they changed up the Pfam entries for those and even created some brand new ones where Pfam was missing information. They've also brought back something called Pfam-B, which is like an extra layer of data; it has 136,730 completely new protein groups that haven’t quite fit into a regular Pfam family yet. This Pfam-B thing uses software called MMseqs2 to group the sequences together.

Plus, they've been comparing everything in RepeatsDB to what’s in Pfam and using those comparisons to build and make the Pfam repeat families even better! You can check out the whole database for free at http://pfam.xfam.org/ – it's really easy to browse and download stuff.

Okay, so back in December 2019, a weird pneumonia popped up in Wuhan – it’s a huge city with about 11 million people and it’s in China. It was caused by a germ we hadn't seen before. Turns out, the first cases were linked to this seafood market they had there. As of January 27th, 2020, China reported over 2,800 confirmed infections – that’s including 81 deaths. But it wasn't just in China; they also found 19 more cases in Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan. And then there were 39 people who had caught it while traveling from places like Thailand, Japan, South Korea, the US, Vietnam, Singapore, Nepal, France, Australia, and Canada. Scientists figured out that this germ was a new type of coronavirus – they called it 2019-nCoV – and it’s really similar to the one that caused SARS back in 2003. Right now, there's no specific medicine to treat it, so people are super worried and trying to find antiviral drugs that will actually work!

formal: In this survey of heath care workers in hospitals equipped with fever clinics or wards for patients with COVID-19 in Wuhan and other regions in China, participants reported experiencing psychological burden, especially nurses, women, those in Wuhan, and frontline health care workers directly engaged in the diagnosis, treatment, and care for patients with COVID-19.
casual: Okay, so basically, this study looked at doctors and nurses working in hospitals across China – mainly in Wuhan and other places – that had special areas for people with fevers or COVID-19. The people taking part in the survey said they were really struggling with their mental health, particularly the nurses, women, those who were based in Wuhan, and all the frontline workers like doctors and nurses who were actually treating patients with COVID-19.

formal: ABSTRACT Radiocarbon ( 14 C) ages cannot provide absolutely dated chronologies for archaeological or paleoenvironmental studies directly but must be converted to calendar age equivalents using a calibration curve compensating for fluctuations in atmospheric 14 C concentration. Although calibration curves are constructed from independently dated archives, they invariably require revision as new data become available and our understanding of the Earth system improves. In this volume the international 14 C calibration curves for both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, as well as for the ocean surface layer, have been updated to include a wealth of new data and extended to 55,000 cal BP. Based on tree rings, IntCal20 now extends as a fully atmospheric record to ca. 13,900 cal BP. For the older part of the timescale, IntCal20 comprises statistically integrated evidence from floating tree-ring chronologies, lacustrine and marine sediments, speleothems, and corals. We utilized improved evaluation of the timescales and location variable 14 C offsets from the atmosphere (reservoir age, dead carbon fraction) for each dataset.
casual:
Okay, so basically, radiocarbon dating – measuring the amount of carbon-14 in something – doesn’t give you a super precise date on its own. It's like having a really good clue, but you need to figure out exactly *when* that clue refers to. You have to use these charts called “calibration curves” to turn those radiocarbon numbers into calendar years. These curves are built from other things we can reliably date, but they’re always getting updated as scientists learn more about how the Earth works and find new information.

This particular study uses the latest versions of those calibration curves for both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, and even the ocean! They've added tons of new data and stretched them back all the way to 55,000 years ago – which is a huge jump from before. The “IntCal20” curve, based on tree ring data, now goes back as far as about 13,900 years. And for dates even older than that, they pulled together information from things like tree rings, lake sediments, cave formations, and coral – all with improved ways of accounting for variations in the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere.

formal: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50.
casual:
Okay, so basically this paper talks about something called SimCLR – it’s a really easy way to teach computers to “see” without needing tons of labeled pictures. It builds on some newer ideas about learning from just your own images, and it doesn’t need any fancy special setups or extra memory. 

The researchers wanted to figure out *why* this method works so well, so they looked closely at the different parts. They found a few key things: first, how you mix up the changes you make to each picture is super important for making good predictions. Second, adding a little flexible adjustment between the image and the way it’s being judged by the learning process really boosted how well the computer learned. And third, contrastive learning – this whole self-supervised thing – actually needs bigger groups of images and more training than regular supervised learning to get the best results. 

Because of all that, SimCLR ended up doing a *lot* better than other methods on ImageNet, beating them by a pretty big margin! A simple classifier using the pictures learned by SimCLR got 76.5% accuracy – that’s way better than what was previously possible, and even matched how well a regular ResNet-50 model trained with labels would do.

formal: In the last few years, the deep learning (DL) computing paradigm has been deemed the Gold Standard in the machine learning (ML) community. Moreover, it has gradually become the most widely used computational approach in the field of ML, thus achieving outstanding results on several complex cognitive tasks, matching or even beating those provided by human performance. One of the benefits of DL is the ability to learn massive amounts of data. The DL field has grown fast in the last few years and it has been extensively used to successfully address a wide range of traditional applications. More importantly, DL has outperformed well-known ML techniques in many domains, e.g., cybersecurity, natural language processing, bioinformatics, robotics and control, and medical information processing, among many others. Despite it has been contributed several works reviewing the State-of-the-Art on DL, all of them only tackled one aspect of the DL, which leads to an overall lack of knowledge about it. Therefore, in this contribution, we propose using a more holistic approach in order to provide a more suitable starting point from which to develop a full understanding of DL.
casual: Okay, so basically, over the last few years, deep learning – or DL – has totally become the top dog in machine learning (ML). It's now *super* popular and it’s actually getting amazing results, sometimes even better than humans, on really tricky problems. One of the coolest things about DL is that it can handle huge amounts of data—like, seriously huge! The field itself has grown so quickly, and people are using it to solve tons of different problems, like old-school stuff but also new ones too. But here's the kicker: DL’s been crushing it compared to older ML methods in areas like cybersecurity, understanding language, figuring out biology, building robots, controlling systems, and even processing medical info – you name it! Despite lots of research looking at DL, most of it just focused on one tiny piece of the puzzle. This left us with a really incomplete picture. So, what we're doing here is taking a bigger, more complete look at DL to help everyone get a solid understanding of how it works and where it’s headed.

formal: The Working Group II contribution to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) provides a comprehensive assessment of the scientific literature relevant to climate change impacts, adaptation and vulnerability. The report recognizes the interactions of climate, ecosystems and biodiversity, and human societies, and integrates across the natural, ecological, social and economic sciences. It emphasizes how efforts in adaptation and in reducing greenhouse gas emissions can come together in a process called climate resilient development, which enables a liveable future for biodiversity and humankind. The IPCC is the leading body for assessing climate change science. IPCC reports are produced in comprehensive, objective and transparent ways, ensuring they reflect the full range of views in the scientific literature. Novel elements include focused topical assessments, and an atlas presenting observed climate change impacts and future risks from global to regional scales. Available as Open Access on Cambridge Core.
casual:
Okay, so basically, the Working Group II part of the IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report is like a huge study looking at *everything* we know about how climate change will affect us – the problems, how we can adapt, and who’s most vulnerable. It really digs into how climate, nature (like plants and animals), and people all connect with each other. They pull in ideas from science like biology, economics, and more. 

The report highlights that if we work on both adapting to change *and* cutting down on greenhouse gases, it’s called “climate-resilient development.” This is key because it helps us make sure there's a future for both wildlife and people! The IPCC is the top group for studying climate science, and their reports are super thorough, honest, and clear – they really look at all the scientific opinions out there. 

Plus, they’ve got some new things like specialized studies on specific topics and even an atlas showing exactly where we're seeing climate change now and what risks might come our way, from huge areas to smaller places. You can find it for free online at Cambridge Core.

formal: Stimulated cells and cancer cells have widespread shortening of mRNA 3'-untranslated regions (3'UTRs) and switches to shorter mRNA isoforms due to usage of more proximal polyadenylation signals (PASs) in introns and last exons. U1 snRNP (U1), vertebrates' most abundant non-coding (spliceosomal) small nuclear RNA, silences proximal PASs and its inhibition with antisense morpholino oligonucleotides (U1 AMO) triggers widespread premature transcription termination and mRNA shortening. Here we show that low U1 AMO doses increase cancer cells' migration and invasion in vitro by up to 500%, whereas U1 over-expression has the opposite effect. In addition to 3'UTR length, numerous transcriptome changes that could contribute to this phenotype are observed, including alternative splicing, and mRNA expression levels of proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressors. These findings reveal an unexpected role for U1 homeostasis (available U1 relative to transcription) in oncogenic and activated cell states, and suggest U1 as a potential target for their modulation.
casual:
Okay, so here’s the breakdown:

Basically, when cells – especially cancer cells – make their messenger RNA (mRNA), they often chop it shorter than usual. They also start using signals closer to where the mRNA is made to tell it how to finish being copied, which leads to smaller versions of the message. U1 snRNP, a really common type of non-coding RNA in our bodies, normally stops these close signals from working. But if we block U1 with a special molecule (U1 AMO), it causes the mRNA to start breaking down way too early and gets much shorter.

We found that using small amounts of this U1 blocker actually makes cancer cells move around and spread out more – up to 500% better in our tests! However, if we add *more* U1 back in, it does the opposite. Plus, when we looked at all the other changes happening in these cells’ genes – like how they change which parts of their messages are used – we saw lots of differences in things like cancer-causing genes and genes that stop cancer from growing. 

It turns out that how much U1 is available compared to how much mRNA is being made plays a big role in whether cells become cancerous or stay healthy. This suggests that controlling U1 could be a way to treat these types of cells.

formal: The aim of the UniProt Knowledgebase is to provide users with a comprehensive, high-quality and freely accessible set of protein sequences annotated with functional information. In this article, we describe significant updates that we have made over the last two years to the resource. The number of sequences in UniProtKB has risen to approximately 190 million, despite continued work to reduce sequence redundancy at the proteome level. We have adopted new methods of assessing proteome completeness and quality. We continue to extract detailed annotations from the literature to add to reviewed entries and supplement these in unreviewed entries with annotations provided by automated systems such as the newly implemented Association-Rule-Based Annotator (ARBA). We have developed a credit-based publication submission interface to allow the community to contribute publications and annotations to UniProt entries. We describe how UniProtKB responded to the COVID-19 pandemic through expert curation of relevant entries that were rapidly made available to the research community through a dedicated portal.
casual:
Okay, so basically, UniProt is this huge database—it’s like a giant library for protein information! The goal is to give everyone super detailed, free access to tons of protein sequences and all the stuff we know about what they actually *do*. We've made some big changes over the past couple of years, and there's now around 190 million proteins listed – even though we’re still working on making sure everything is unique.  

We've gotten better at figuring out how complete our database is and how good the information actually is. We keep digging through research papers to add details to existing entries, and we also use computer programs like ARBA to help fill in gaps, especially for proteins where we don’t have as much info yet.  

Plus, we've created a system where researchers can submit their own publications and annotations directly into the database – it's all based on points! And, during the COVID-19 pandemic, we quickly added information about relevant proteins through a special portal to help scientists get the data they needed really fast.

formal: The PRoteomics IDEntifications (PRIDE) database (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/) is the world's largest data repository of mass spectrometry-based proteomics data. PRIDE is one of the founding members of the global ProteomeXchange (PX) consortium and an ELIXIR core data resource. In this manuscript, we summarize the developments in PRIDE resources and related tools since the previous update manuscript was published in Nucleic Acids Research in 2019. The number of submitted datasets to PRIDE Archive (the archival component of PRIDE) has reached on average around 500 datasets per month during 2021. In addition to continuous improvements in PRIDE Archive data pipelines and infrastructure, the PRIDE Spectra Archive has been developed to provide direct access to the submitted mass spectra using Universal Spectrum Identifiers. As a key point, the file format MAGE-TAB for proteomics has been developed to enable the improvement of sample metadata annotation. Additionally, the resource PRIDE Peptidome provides access to aggregated peptide/protein evidences across PRIDE Archive.
casual: Okay, so basically, the PRIDE database (you can find it at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/) is like the biggest library ever for mass spec data – seriously, it’s got tons of proteomics info! It's also one of the original creators of ProteomeXchange (PX), and they’re even a core part of something called ELIXIR, which helps with scientific data. This paper basically tells us about all the new stuff that’s been added to PRIDE since 2019. During 2021 alone, they were getting, on average, around 500 new datasets uploaded every month to their main archive! They've also been constantly making improvements to how the data gets stored and organized. Plus, they built a separate thing called the Spectra Archive – it lets you get right to the mass spectra themselves using special identifiers. Importantly, they created something called MAGE-TAB, which is a file format designed to make labeling samples way easier. And finally, there’s this resource called PRIDE Peptidome that pulls together all the evidence for peptides and proteins from across the entire database – pretty cool, right?

formal: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.
casual:
Okay, so basically, most really good translation models used to be super complicated – they’d use these long, looping networks (recurrent) or grids of calculations (convolutions) to turn one language into another. The best ones even added something called “attention,” which helped them focus on the right parts of the sentence. But we came up with a new idea: the Transformer! It's *just* based on attention, ditching all the loops and grids completely. 

We tested it out on two translation jobs – English to German and English to French – and guess what? It did way better than anything else, like over 2 points higher on a score called BLEU (which basically measures how good the translation is). On the German job, we got 28.4 BLEU, beating everyone, even groups of models working together! And on the French job, it scored an amazing 41.8 – and we only trained it for about 3.5 days using eight computers, which is way cheaper than other top-performing systems. 

The cool thing is, this Transformer also works really well for other things too – like figuring out how sentences are structured (English constituency parsing) – even with lots or just a little bit of training data!

formal: An outbreak of novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV) that began in Wuhan, China, has spread rapidly, with cases now confirmed in multiple countries. We report the first case of 2019-nCoV infection confirmed in the United States and describe the identification, diagnosis, clinical course, and management of the case, including the patient's initial mild symptoms at presentation with progression to pneumonia on day 9 of illness. This case highlights the importance of close coordination between clinicians and public health authorities at the local, state, and federal levels, as well as the need for rapid dissemination of clinical information related to the care of patients with this emerging infection.
casual: Okay, so there’s been this really fast-spreading illness called the novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV) that started in Wuhan, China – and it's now popping up all over the world. We wanted to share about the very first time we saw this virus in the US. Basically, we found someone who was infected, and we tracked everything about their case: how they were diagnosed, how sick they got, and how we treated them. They started out with just some mild symptoms at first, but then by day nine, it had turned into pneumonia. It really shows how important it is for doctors, public health folks (at all levels – local, state, federal), and everyone to work together quickly. And, of course, getting the word out about what we’re learning about treating this new infection as fast as possible is super crucial.

formal: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in over 4.3 million confirmed cases and over 290,000 deaths globally. It has also sparked fears of an impending economic crisis and recession. Social distancing, self-isolation and travel restrictions have lead to a reduced workforce across all economic sectors and caused many jobs to be lost. Schools have closed down, and the need for commodities and manufactured products has decreased. In contrast, the need for medical supplies has significantly increased. The food sector is also facing increased demand due to panic-buying and stockpiling of food products. In response to this global outbreak, we summarise the socio-economic effects of COVID-19 on individual aspects of the world economy.
casual:
Okay, so basically, the whole COVID-19 thing has been *huge*. There have been over 4.3 million people confirmed as having it, and sadly, more than 290,000 deaths worldwide – a really serious number. It’s also made everyone worried about a major economic crash and a recession coming.

Because of everything—like social distancing and people staying home—a lot fewer people are working across almost every industry, which means tons of jobs have disappeared. Schools shut down, and things like regular products just aren't being bought as much anymore. But crazy enough, demand for stuff like masks, ventilators, and other medical supplies has skyrocketed! 

Even the food industry is feeling it because people were going nuts buying up everything and hoarding food – so there’s way more demand than usual. Basically, we wanted to break down all the different ways this pandemic has hit the world economy.

formal: An unprecedented outbreak of pneumonia of unknown aetiology in Wuhan City, Hubei province in China emerged in December 2019. A novel coronavirus was identified as the causative agent and was subsequently termed COVID-19 by the World Health Organization (WHO). Considered a relative of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), COVID-19 is caused by a betacoronavirus named SARS-CoV-2 that affects the lower respiratory tract and manifests as pneumonia in humans. Despite rigorous global containment and quarantine efforts, the incidence of COVID-19 continues to rise, with 90,870 laboratory-confirmed cases and over 3,000 deaths worldwide. In response to this global outbreak, we summarise the current state of knowledge surrounding COVID-19.
casual: Okay, so basically, back in December 2019, there was this crazy sudden pneumonia outbreak happening in Wuhan, China – it was totally baffling because nobody knew what was causing it. Scientists figured out it was a brand-new coronavirus and they called it COVID-19 after the World Health Organization (WHO). It’s similar to illnesses like SARS and MERS, which are also caused by coronaviruses. Specifically, this one is from a type of coronavirus called SARS-CoV-2, and it mainly hits your lungs, leading to pneumonia. Even though people worked super hard to contain it with quarantines and stuff, the number of cases keeps going up – there have been over 90,870 confirmed cases worldwide now, and sadly, more than 3,000 deaths. We’re just trying to get a clear picture of what we know about COVID-19 right now because it's such a big problem.

formal: This review is an updated and expanded version of the five prior reviews that were published in this journal in 1997, 2003, 2007, 2012, and 2016. For all approved therapeutic agents, the time frame has been extended to cover the almost 39 years from the first of January 1981 to the 30th of September 2019 for all diseases worldwide and from ∼1946 (earliest so far identified) to the 30th of September 2019 for all approved antitumor drugs worldwide. As in earlier reviews, only the first approval of any drug is counted, irrespective of how many "biosimilars" or added approvals were subsequently identified. As in the 2012 and 2016 reviews, we have continued to utilize our secondary subdivision of a "natural product mimic", or "NM", to join the original primary divisions, and the designation "natural product botanical", or "NB", to cover those botanical "defined mixtures" now recognized as drug entities by the FDA (and similar organizations). From the data presented in this review, the utilization of natural products and/or synthetic variations using their novel structures, in order to discover and develop the final drug entity, is still alive and well.
casual: Okay, so basically, this article is a big update – it’s taken everything from five older reviews published back in 1997, 2003, 2007, 2012, and 2016, and built on it. It looks at treatments for almost 40 years, starting January 1st, 1981, and going all the way to September 30th, 2019, for pretty much every disease around the world. And for cancer drugs, it goes back as far as 1946! Now, we only count when a drug was *first* approved – even if there were later versions or “copycat” drugs made afterward. Like in those earlier reviews, and also in 2012 and 2016, we’ve added a new section about "natural product mimics" (NM) and “natural product botanicals” (NB) to cover things like herbal mixtures that are now considered medicines by the FDA. The whole point is that using natural products – or making similar versions of them – to find and create these drugs is still happening today!

formal: Abstract The Review summarizes much of particle physics and cosmology. Using data from previous editions, plus 2,143 new measurements from 709 papers, we list, evaluate, and average measured properties of gauge bosons and the recently discovered Higgs boson, leptons, quarks, mesons, and baryons. We summarize searches for hypothetical particles such as supersymmetric particles, heavy bosons, axions, dark photons, etc. Particle properties and search limits are listed in Summary Tables. We give numerous tables, figures, formulae, and reviews of topics such as Higgs Boson Physics, Supersymmetry, Grand Unified Theories, Neutrino Mixing, Dark Energy, Dark Matter, Cosmology, Particle Detectors, Colliders, Probability and Statistics. Among the 120 reviews are many that are new or heavily revised, including a new review on Machine Learning, and one on Spectroscopy of Light Meson Resonances. The Review is divided into two volumes. Volume 1 includes the Summary Tables and 97 review articles. Volume 2 consists of the Particle Listings and contains also 23 reviews that address specific aspects of the data presented in the Listings.
casual:
Okay, so basically this huge report is like a super-detailed look at pretty much all of modern particle physics and cosmology. It takes everything we knew before and adds in over 2,100 new measurements – they pulled data from 709 different research papers! They then carefully checked out and combined information about things like gauge bosons (those force carriers), the Higgs boson, leptons, quarks, mesons, baryons, and even looked for these really hypothetical particles like supersymmetric stuff or axions.

They’ve made tons of tables and charts to show all the measurements and how good they are, along with lots of explanations on topics such as the Higgs Boson, Supersymmetry, Grand Unified Theories, how neutrinos mix, dark energy, dark matter – you name it!  A bunch of these explanations were updated or even brand new, including a review about using machine learning.

The whole thing is split into two volumes. Volume 1 has all the main tables and around 97 reviews that go over the basics. Volume 2 then breaks down the specific data they collected, with another 23 reviews focusing on details from those listings.

formal: In December, 2019, a local outbreak of pneumonia of initially unknown cause was detected in Wuhan (Hubei, China), and was quickly determined to be caused by a novel coronavirus,1WHOWHO statement regarding cluster of pneumonia cases in Wuhan, China.https://www.who.int/china/news/detail/09-01-2020-who-statement-regarding-cluster-of-pneumonia-cases-in-wuhan-chinaDate: Jan 9, 2020Date accessed: February 11, 2020Google Scholar namely severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The outbreak has since spread to every province of mainland China as well as 27 other countries and regions, with more than 70 000 confirmed cases as of Feb 17, 2020.2WHOCoronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) situation reports.https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/situation-reportsDate accessed: February 17, 2020Google Scholar In response to this ongoing public health emergency, we developed an online interactive dashboard, hosted by the Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) at Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA, to visualise and track reported cases of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in real time.
casual:
Okay, so back in December 2019, doctors noticed a bunch of people in Wuhan, China – specifically in the Hubei province – were getting really sick with pneumonia.
