It lets you see exactly where the COVID-19 cases are popping up.

formal: The latest JBI guidance for scoping reviews provides up-to-date guidance that can be used by authors when conducting a scoping review. Furthermore, it aligns with the PRISMA-ScR, which can be used to report the conduct of a scoping review. A series of ongoing and future methodological projects identified by the JBI Scoping Review Methodology Group to further refine the methodology are planned.
casual: Okay, so basically, the newest advice from JBI on doing scoping reviews is super helpful for anyone writing one – it gives you all the details you need. It also matches up with something called PRISMA-ScR, which is a way to clearly show how your scoping review was done. And, JBI’s team is still working on making these guidelines even better through some ongoing projects and plans for future improvements!

formal: AutoDock Vina is arguably one of the fastest and most widely used open-source programs for molecular docking. However, compared to other programs in the AutoDock Suite, it lacks support for modeling specific features such as macrocycles or explicit water molecules. Here, we describe the implementation of these functionality in AutoDock Vina 1.2.0. Additionally, AutoDock Vina 1.2.0 supports the AutoDock4.2 scoring function, simultaneous docking of multiple ligands, and a batch mode for docking a large number of ligands. Furthermore, we implemented Python bindings to facilitate scripting and the development of docking workflows. This work is an effort toward the unification of the features of the AutoDock4 and AutoDock Vina programs. The source code is available at https://github.com/ccsb-scripps/AutoDock-Vina
casual:
Okay, so AutoDock Vina is pretty awesome – it’s super fast and tons of people use it for predicting how molecules fit together. But, honestly, it doesn't do *everything*. Unlike some other programs in the AutoDock family, it doesn’t automatically handle things like really big rings (macrocycles) or adding water molecules to the calculations. 

We fixed that! In this version of AutoDock Vina (1.2.0), we added support for those macrocycles and water – so you can get more accurate results. Plus, it now works with the newer AutoDock4.2 scoring function, lets you dock lots of different molecules at once, and even has a “batch mode” to handle tons of them all together. 

To make things easier, we also created Python scripts, which means you can build your own automated docking workflows. Basically, this whole project is about bringing the AutoDock4 and Vina programs closer together – making everything work smoothly! You can find the code itself on GitHub: https://github.com/ccsb-scripps/AutoDock-Vina

formal: Background Chest CT is used in the diagnosis of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and is an important complement to reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests. Purpose To investigate the diagnostic value and consistency of chest CT as compared with RT-PCR assay in COVID-19. Materials and Methods This study included 1014 patients in Wuhan, China, who underwent both chest CT and RT-PCR tests between January 6 and February 6, 2020. With use of RT-PCR as the reference standard, the performance of chest CT in the diagnosis of COVID-19 was assessed. In addition, for patients with multiple RT-PCR assays, the dynamic conversion of RT-PCR results (negative to positive, positive to negative) was analyzed as compared with serial chest CT scans for those with a time interval between RT-PCR tests of 4 days or more. Results Of the 1014 patients, 601 of 1014 (59%) had positive RT-PCR results and 888 of 1014 (88%) had positive chest CT scans. The sensitivity of chest CT in suggesting COVID-19 was 97% (95% confidence interval: 95%, 98%; 580 of 601 patients) based on positive RT-PCR results.
casual:
Okay, so basically, doctors use chest CT scans to check for COVID-19 – and they’re really helpful alongside those standard RT-PCR tests. The goal of this study was to see how well chest CT scans matched up with the RT-PCR tests in diagnosing the illness.

They looked at 1014 people in Wuhan, China, who had both a chest CT scan *and* an RT-PCR test done between January and February of 2020. They used the RT-PCR results as the main way to check if something was wrong.  

Here’s what they found: A whopping 601 out of those 1014 people (that's about 59%) had positive RT-PCR results, meaning they really did have COVID-19. And even more – 888 out of 1014 (or 88%) showed up with positive chest CT scans!

The chest CT scan was super accurate; it correctly flagged COVID-19 in 97% of the cases where the RT-PCR test came back positive. That's a really high number – over 580 out of those 601 people with positive RT-PCR results.

formal: DAVID is a popular bioinformatics resource system including a web server and web service for functional annotation and enrichment analyses of gene lists. It consists of a comprehensive knowledgebase and a set of functional analysis tools. Here, we report all updates made in 2021. The DAVID Gene system was rebuilt to gain coverage of more organisms, which increased the taxonomy coverage from 17 399 to 55 464. All existing annotation types have been updated, if available, based on the new DAVID Gene system. Compared with the last version, the number of gene-term records for most annotation types within the updated Knowledgebase have significantly increased. Moreover, we have incorporated new annotations in the Knowledgebase including small molecule-gene interactions from PubChem, drug-gene interactions from DrugBank, tissue expression information from the Human Protein Atlas, disease information from DisGeNET, and pathways from WikiPathways and PathBank. Eight of ten subgroups split from Uniprot Keyword annotation were assigned to specific types.
casual:
Okay, so basically, DAVID is this super popular tool for biologists – it’s like a website and service that helps you understand what your genes *do*. It uses a huge database packed with tools for analyzing gene lists.

In 2021, they totally revamped the whole system! They added coverage for way more organisms; it went from recognizing data for 17,399 to now covering 55,464 different species – that’s a massive jump! And they updated all the existing ways they could, using the new DAVID Gene system.

As a result, there are *way* more connections between genes and what they mean (called “gene-term records”) in the database for most of those categories. Plus, they added some seriously cool new information: things like how small molecules interact with genes (thanks to PubChem), drug interactions with genes (from DrugBank), tissue expression data (from the Human Protein Atlas), disease info (from DisGeNET), and pathways (from WikiPathways and PathBank). They even sorted out eight out of ten groups that came from Uniprot Keyword annotations, giving them specific labels.

formal: The ESC Guidelines represent the views of the ESC and were produced after careful consideration of the scientific and medical knowledge and the evidence available at the time of their publication. The ESC is not responsible in the event of any contradiction, discrepancy and/or ambiguity between the ESC Guidelines and any other official recommendations or guidelines issued by the relevant public health authorities, in particular in relation to good use of healthcare or therapeutic strategies. Health professionals are encouraged to take the ESC Guidelines fully into account when exercising their clinical judgment, as well as in the determination and the implementation of preventive, diagnostic or therapeutic medical strategies; however, the ESC Guidelines do not override, in any way whatsoever, the individual responsibility of health professionals to make appropriate and accurate decisions in consideration of each patient's health condition and in consultation with that patient and, where appropriate and/or necessary, the patient's caregiver.
casual: Okay, so basically, the ESC’s guidelines are just what they thought was best based on all the science and research when they wrote them. They aren’t saying these are the *only* rules—they recognize that other health groups might have different ideas too, especially about how healthcare should be used. Doctors should definitely use these guidelines as a guide when making decisions for their patients, you know, like figuring out what tests to do or what treatments to try. But here’s the key: doctors still have to think for themselves and consider each patient's unique situation – seriously, it’s about using the guidelines *along with* their own judgment and talking to the patient (and their family if they need to) every step of the way.

formal: The Working Group I contribution to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) provides a comprehensive assessment of the physical science basis of climate change. It considers in situ and remote observations; paleoclimate information; understanding of climate drivers and physical, chemical, and biological processes and feedbacks; global and regional climate modelling; advances in methods of analyses; and insights from climate services. It assesses the current state of the climate; human influence on climate in all regions; future climate change including sea level rise; global warming effects including extremes; climate information for risk assessment and regional adaptation; limiting climate change by reaching net zero carbon dioxide emissions and reducing other greenhouse gas emissions; and benefits for air quality. The report serves policymakers, decision makers, stakeholders, and all interested parties with the latest policy-relevant information on climate change. Available as Open Access on Cambridge Core.
casual:
Okay, so basically, the Working Group I report for the IPCC’s Sixth Assessment really breaks down everything we know about how climate change works physically. They looked at tons of stuff – like data from scientists who actually went out into the field and satellites, plus records from way back in history. Plus, they dug deep into all the different forces driving climate, how things like chemistry and biology play a role, and how those systems interact with each other.

They also used powerful computer models to simulate the climate and kept improving their methods for analyzing data. And importantly, they took what experts were saying about climate services – you know, practical advice for dealing with climate change. 

What they found is pretty clear: humans are causing climate change all over the globe, and it's leading to things like rising sea levels and more extreme weather events. They’re also giving us information we can use to figure out how climate change will affect specific areas and help communities prepare.  It’s about cutting down on carbon dioxide emissions – basically aiming for “net zero” – plus reducing other greenhouse gases too.  And, as a bonus, tackling climate change actually makes the air cleaner! 

This report is packed with info that helps people in charge – like politicians and decision-makers – understand what’s going on and make smart choices about how to respond. You can find it for free online at Cambridge Core.

formal: Many real-world applications require the prediction of long sequence time-series, such as electricity consumption planning. Long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) demands a high prediction capacity of the model, which is the ability to capture precise long-range dependency coupling between output and input efficiently. Recent studies have shown the potential of Transformer to increase the prediction capacity. However, there are several severe issues with Transformer that prevent it from being directly applicable to LSTF, including quadratic time complexity, high memory usage, and inherent limitation of the encoder-decoder architecture. To address these issues, we design an efficient transformer-based model for LSTF, named Informer, with three distinctive characteristics: (i) a ProbSparse self-attention mechanism, which achieves O(L log L) in time complexity and memory usage, and has comparable performance on sequences' dependency alignment. (ii) the self-attention distilling highlights dominating attention by halving cascading layer input, and efficiently handles extreme long input sequences.
casual: Okay, so basically, a lot of real jobs need us to guess how things will change over time – like predicting how much electricity people will use. When we’re looking at really long stretches of data like that, it's called “long sequence time-series forecasting,” and the models have to be *really* good at spotting patterns that stretch way back in time. Scientists are finding that Transformers can do a better job with this, but there are some big problems with them. They take a ton of computing power, use lots of memory, and the way they're built just isn’t great for these really long sequences. That’s why we came up with Informer – it’s a smarter version that uses a special attention thing called “ProbSparse.” This makes it much faster and more efficient, working on about half the amount of data while still getting good results at understanding how things are connected over time. Plus, it can handle super-long sequences without struggling!

formal: The UK Medical Research Council’s widely used guidance for developing and evaluating complex interventions has been replaced by a new framework, commissioned jointly by the Medical Research Council and the National Institute for Health Research, which takes account of recent developments in theory and methods and the need to maximise the efficiency, use, and impact of research.
casual: Okay, so basically, the old rules researchers followed from the UK’s Medical Research Council – they've been updated! The MRC and the National Institute for Health Research teamed up to create a new framework. It’s designed to make sure we’re doing research that’s actually useful and effective, considering all the latest ideas about how things work and how best to get the most out of our studies.

formal: The asymmetric α-addition of relatively nonpolar hydrocarbon substrates, such as allyl and aryl groups, to aldehydes and ketones remains a largely unsolved problem in organic synthesis, despite the wide potential utility of direct routes to such products. We reasoned that well-established chiral amine catalysis, which activates aldehydes toward electrophile addition by enamine formation, could be expanded to this important reaction class by applying a single-electron oxidant to create a transient radical species from the enamine. We demonstrated the concept of singly occupied molecular orbital (SOMO) activation with a highly selective α-allylation of aldehydes, and we here present preliminary results for enantioselective heteroarylations and cyclization/halogenation cascades.
casual:
Okay, so basically, it’s really tricky to add things like “allyl” or “aryl” groups – which are pretty non-polar – to things like aldehydes and ketones in a way that makes sense. Scientists have been trying to figure this out for ages, even though it could be super useful to make these products directly. 

Here's the idea: they thought about how chiral amines already work really well at helping aldehydes react with other stuff. They do this by making an “enamine,” which basically gets the aldehyde ready for a reaction. So, they figured they could use a little bit of an oxidant – something that gives off a single electron – to turn that enamine into a temporary radical. This is like activating it! 

They showed it works really well with just one allylation (adding an allyl group), and now they’re starting to test it out for adding other things, too, like heteroaryls, and even for making complicated rings or doing reactions that involve both halogenation and cyclization – pretty cool stuff!

formal: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) is the cellular receptor for severe acute respiratory syndrome-coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and the new coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) that is causing the serious coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) epidemic. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of full-length human ACE2 in the presence of the neutral amino acid transporter B<sup>0</sup>AT1 with or without the receptor binding domain (RBD) of the surface spike glycoprotein (S protein) of SARS-CoV-2, both at an overall resolution of 2.9 angstroms, with a local resolution of 3.5 angstroms at the ACE2-RBD interface. The ACE2-B<sup>0</sup>AT1 complex is assembled as a dimer of heterodimers, with the collectrin-like domain of ACE2 mediating homodimerization. The RBD is recognized by the extracellular peptidase domain of ACE2 mainly through polar residues. These findings provide important insights into the molecular basis for coronavirus recognition and infection.
casual:
Okay, so basically, this protein called ACE2 – Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 – is super important because it’s like a doorway that COVID-19 uses to get inside our cells. SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2, the viruses causing COVID-19, actually latch onto ACE2 to spread.

We got really detailed pictures using something called cryo-electron microscopy. These images show how full-length human ACE2 works when it’s teamed up with another protein called B0AT1 – it's like a helper. We looked at this team both with and without the “RBD” part of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which is a key piece that grabs onto ACE2. The pictures were really clear – around 2.9 angstroms, with even more detail at the spot where ACE2 and RBD connect (3.5 angstroms).

It turns out, ACE2 teams up with B0AT1 to form these little clumps that are like two connected structures. A protein called collectrin-like stuff helps those clumps stick together. The RBD – that part of the virus – is mainly recognized by the outside part of ACE2 because of some special polar chemicals. 

So, this research really explains how coronaviruses find and invade our cells!

formal: DiffuCpG 1. Introduction In this study, we used a generative AI diffusion model to address missing methylation data. We trained the model with Whole-Genome Bisulfite Sequencing data from 26 acute myeloid leukemia samples and validated it with Reduced Representation Bisulfite Sequencing data from 93 myelodysplastic syndrome and 13 normal samples. Additional testing included data from the Illumina 450k methylation array and Single-Cell Reduced Representation Bisulfite Sequencing on HepG2 cells. Our model, DiffuCpG, outperformed previous methods by integrating a broader range of genomic features, utilizing both short- and long-range interactions without increasing input complexity. It demonstrated superior accuracy, scalability, and versatility across various tissues, diseases, and technologies, providing predictions in both binary and continuous methylation states. In this repository, we deposit the code used to build the diffusion models along with necessary example datasets to train and test a diffusion model for methylation imputation purposes.
casual:
Okay, so basically, we built this cool AI tool called DiffuCpG to figure out missing DNA methylation information – think of it like filling in gaps in a really detailed puzzle. We started by training it on some pretty intense data: whole-genome bisulfite sequencing from 26 leukemia samples. Then, we checked if it worked well with smaller amounts of bisulfite sequencing data from 93 myelodysplastic syndrome cases and 13 normal cells.  

We also tested it out using older methylation array data (from the Illumina 450k) and even some single-cell bisulfite sequencing on liver cells (HepG2). The really neat thing about DiffuCpG is that it was way better than other methods – it could handle a lot more information and looked at connections between DNA bits both close together and far apart, without making things super complicated. 

It worked great across different kinds of tissues, diseases, and even with different types of tests, giving us predictions for whether methylation levels were high or low. You can find all the code we used to build this thing, plus some example datasets, in this repository – so you can try it out yourself and see how it works for filling in those missing methylation spots!

formal: Tumor progression and the efficacy of immunotherapy are strongly influenced by the composition and abundance of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment. Due to the limitations of direct measurement methods, computational algorithms are often used to infer immune cell composition from bulk tumor transcriptome profiles. These estimated tumor immune infiltrate populations have been associated with genomic and transcriptomic changes in the tumors, providing insight into tumor-immune interactions. However, such investigations on large-scale public data remain challenging. To lower the barriers for the analysis of complex tumor-immune interactions, we significantly improved our previous web platform TIMER. Instead of just using one algorithm, TIMER2.0 (http://timer.cistrome.org/) provides more robust estimation of immune infiltration levels for The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) or user-provided tumor profiles using six state-of-the-art algorithms. TIMER2.0 provides four modules for investigating the associations between immune infiltrates and genetic or clinical features, and four modules for exploring cancer-related associations in the TCGA cohorts.
casual:
Okay, so basically, how quickly a tumor grows and whether immunotherapy works really depends on what kinds of immune cells are hanging out inside it – specifically, *how many* there are. It’s tricky to actually count them directly, though, which is why scientists often use computer programs to guess at the makeup of these immune cell groups based on information from the whole tumor's genes (called a transcriptome profile).  

These estimated numbers of immune cells have been linked to changes in the tumor itself and how it interacts with the immune system – that’s pretty cool! But, looking at this kind of data across huge public datasets like The Cancer Genome Atlas is really hard. 

That's why they made a big upgrade to their old website, TIMER2.0 (you can find it at http://timer.cistrome.org/). Instead of just one program, it uses six super-smart algorithms to get a much better read on immune cell levels in tumors from the TCGA database or even your own tumor samples. 

TIMER2.0 has four different tools you can use: one to see how immune cells relate to things like genes and patient health, and another four to explore connections between cancer characteristics within the TCGA data – it’s a really powerful tool for digging into these complex tumor-immune relationships!

formal: The Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project was established to characterize genetic effects on the transcriptome across human tissues and to link these regulatory mechanisms to trait and disease associations. Here, we present analyses of the version 8 data, examining 15,201 RNA-sequencing samples from 49 tissues of 838 postmortem donors. We comprehensively characterize genetic associations for gene expression and splicing in cis and trans, showing that regulatory associations are found for almost all genes, and describe the underlying molecular mechanisms and their contribution to allelic heterogeneity and pleiotropy of complex traits. Leveraging the large diversity of tissues, we provide insights into the tissue specificity of genetic effects and show that cell type composition is a key factor in understanding gene regulatory mechanisms in human tissues.
casual: Okay, so basically, the GTEx project was set up to figure out how our genes actually affect what’s going on with our bodies – specifically, all the different types of RNA – in various human tissues. They wanted to connect these genetic things to diseases and conditions.  They looked at data from version 8, which included results from over 15,000 RNA sequencing tests done on samples from 49 different tissues, taken from 838 people who had passed away. What they found was pretty amazing: almost *every* gene has a genetic link to how it’s expressed or how it's spliced (which is a complicated way of saying how our bodies use the genes). They also saw that these genetic links can affect things like different versions of a gene appearing in people – which is called allelic heterogeneity – and can even explain why one gene seems to cause multiple problems.  Because they had so many different tissues, they were able to really understand how genes act differently depending on the tissue type. They discovered that the mix of different cell types within each tissue plays a huge role in figuring out exactly how genes are controlled in our bodies.

formal: Genetic variants that inactivate protein-coding genes are a powerful source of information about the phenotypic consequences of gene disruption: genes that are crucial for the function of an organism will be depleted of such variants in natural populations, whereas non-essential genes will tolerate their accumulation. However, predicted loss-of-function variants are enriched for annotation errors, and tend to be found at extremely low frequencies, so their analysis requires careful variant annotation and very large sample sizes<sup>1</sup>. Here we describe the aggregation of 125,748 exomes and 15,708 genomes from human sequencing studies into the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD). We identify 443,769 high-confidence predicted loss-of-function variants in this cohort after filtering for artefacts caused by sequencing and annotation errors. Using an improved model of human mutation rates, we classify human protein-coding genes along a spectrum that represents tolerance to inactivation, validate this classification using data from model organisms and engineered human cells, and show that it can be used to improve the power of gene discovery for both common and rare diseases.
casual:
Okay, so basically, when a gene stops working – like gets turned off – it gives us *tons* of clues about what makes an organism tick and how genes affect things like health. Genes we really need to function are usually super clean; you don’t see many changes messing with them in real people. But, predicting which genes might stop working is tricky! These predictions often have mistakes attached to them, they're rare, and we need *lots* of data to be sure about them <supหมายเหตุ 1</sup>.

We put together a huge collection – 125,748 exomes (parts of DNA) and 15,708 full genomes – from lots of people’s DNA sequences, and called it the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD). We found over 443,000 genes that we think might stop working when a change happens. We cleaned up the data by getting rid of errors caused by how we read the DNA and by checking the annotations too.

Then, using a better way to figure out how likely a gene is to stop working, we ranked all the human genes from most tolerant to least tolerant – like a scale! We checked our work with similar genes in other animals and even in cells we made ourselves, and it worked really well.  This system actually helps us find genes linked to diseases, both common ones and rare ones, much faster!

formal: Used to work in the salt industry ( yes , it 's a thing ) . Salt is one of the cheapest substances on earth . As in , you 'd be getting ripped off if you paid more than $ 150 per metric ton . Its crystalline structure can also be manipulated in order to have sharper edges that reduce bounce . So that allows it to stick evenly to critical surfaces such as roads . Yes , there are alternatives . Usually salt / gravel mix or sugar beet based solutions . Those have less of an environmental impact when the spring melt washes it into the drain . This is more used in places where balance of water salinity for the safety of aquatic life is important . formal: There are a few reasons why SD channels still exist : 1 ) SD channels typically consume much less bandwidth than HD channels , so it is possible to carry many more SD channels than HD channels over the same coaxial cable or wireless spectrum ( for antenna broadcasts ) . This point does not apply when a television service provider carries both HD and SD versions of the same channel though . 2 ) Broadcasts formatted for HDTVs ( in 16x9 aspect ratio ) will typically have important details / information cut - off if displayed on an older 4:3 television screens . The SD - specific channels are often formatted especially for older 4:3 screens so that important graphics / information / details etc . do n't get cut - off . 3 ) Not all TVs / tuners are capable of receiving HD broadcasts even though they may be capable of receiving digital SD broadcasts . 4 ) With respect to cable TV , some cable companies still carry analog SD channels which can be received by older television sets without the need of a digital - to - analog adapter .
casual: Okay, so there are a few reasons why you still see those old SD channels around. First off, they use way less data than HD channels – that means you can fit tons more of them over something like an antenna or cable. But this doesn’t matter if your TV provider is also showing HD versions of the same channel. Second, when TVs are made for widescreen HDTVs (like 16x9), a lot of the smaller details get cut off when you watch them on older, squarer TVs. SD channels were often designed specifically for those older 4:3 screens so all the important graphics and info wouldn’t disappear! Also, not every TV or receiver can handle HD broadcasts – some are still set up to just pick up regular SD signals. And finally, with cable TV, some companies still keep around old analog SD channels that your really old TVs can watch without needing a special adapter.

formal: This is a frequent phenomenon with technology : something is considered very hard or even impossible for a long , long time , and then one day , somebody figures it out . That opens a whole FLOODGATE of discovery leading to discovery , and the technology leaps forward quickly . Eventually , those chains of discovery start to play out , and the rate of advancement slows down , and may even come to a halt , perhaps starting up again years later when somebody discovers something new . We saw the same phenomenon with the building of the first transistor in 1947 . The * theory * of transistors had actually been known since the early 20th century , but nobody had figured out a way to actually build one . That led to an explosion in electronics , and when somebody figured out how to put a shitload of teensy transistors on a silicon wafer , the explosion exploded .
casual: Okay, so you see this *all* the time with tech – something seems totally impossible for ages, right? Then suddenly, someone cracks it. And that just opens up like a crazy flood of new ideas and discoveries, which makes technology move forward super fast. Eventually though, all those discoveries start to run their course, and things slow down—sometimes even stop completely! It could take years before someone else finds something new to kick things off again. We saw this happen when they first built the first transistor back in 1947. The basic idea behind transistors had been around since the early 1900s, but nobody knew how to actually *build* one. That led to a huge boom in electronics, and once people figured out how to cram tons of tiny transistors onto a piece of silicon, well… it was like an explosion!

formal: Melanin ! Many of the the first known humans existed in the fertile crescent - modern day Iraq and surrounding areas , and it was just as sunny and hot as it is today . A long time ago, when our earliest ancestors lived in places like Iraq – you know, the Fertile Crescent – it was super sunny and hot, just like it is now! Melanin is what makes your skin and eyes darker; basically, it helps protect you from too much sun. It blocks a bunch of harmful UV rays from getting into your skin. As people moved to cooler, less sunny spots, folks with lighter skin and eyes were able to survive and have kids because they didn't need as much melanin for protection anymore – it was an advantage!

formal: EDIT , Nov 21 : By popular demand , now includes Midrange decks and Limited formats . Also , a new section on where players get their cards . Magic : The Gathering is a collectable card game . It can be played in several different formats , but in the most common , two players create decks out of the cards they own and play against each other . Generally , the cards in a deck are either lands or spells . Lands provide the energy needed to cast spells , and spells usually do one of the following : - Summon a creature that can fight for you or an artifact that you can use . ( * * Creatures * * and * * Artifacts * * ) - Create a lasting effect that affects the game as a whole or one or more cards in play . ( * * Enchantments * * ) - Create an instantaneous effect that affects one or more cards in play or an effect that lasts a single turn . ( * * Sorceries * * and * * Instants * * ) - Summon a sort of " teammate " that has its own abilities . ( * * Planeswalkers * * ) The primary goal is to run your opponent out of life points by attacking him with creatures or damaging him directly with spells . There are other ways to win , such as running your opponent out of cards in his deck .
casual:

formal: Like viruses , they are ( groups of ) molecules that reproduce without metabolism . Unlike any other self - replicating system , prions are proteins that have a unique structure . One part of how a protein functions is the amino acid sequence that makes up the primary structure , but the other part is how the proteins folds , either by itself or with the help of other folder - helper proteins . Prions have the same amino acid sequence as their properly folded brethren , but they are folded differently , and they make a chain reaction by folding their brethren to be like them . Cruetzfeld - Jakob disease in humans , Mad Cow disease in cows , and chronic wasting disease in deer , are all prion diseases that affect neuronal proteins .
casual: Okay, so basically, these things – we call them prions – are like viruses, but they’re made of just molecules instead of being alive. They can copy themselves over and over again without needing to eat or use energy, which is pretty wild! What's really strange about prions is that they're just proteins, and they have this super unique shape. Normally, a protein works because of its building blocks – the specific order of amino acids, called the primary structure. But proteins also fold up into different shapes, sometimes on their own or with the help of other helper proteins. Prions look almost exactly the same as normal proteins in terms of their building blocks, but they’re folded differently. They actually cause a chain reaction where they make *other* proteins fold up like them too! We see this happen in diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in people, Mad Cow disease in cows, and chronic wasting disease in deer – all of these are caused by problems with the proteins in nerve cells.

casual:
Okay, so basically, your brain and body are *always* working to get everything back to what it considers “normal.” And this normal isn’t set in stone; it changes constantly based on your DNA and RNA – think of them like your personal fingerprints that keep updating.

When something new happens – whether it's a physical sensation or a thought – your brain checks it against all the stuff you’ve learned over time. It basically looks for similar experiences from your past to see if they match up. Little differences might just be because you're waking up and your short-term memory is fresh, but that only matters for things you’ve learned recently, like since your last dream.

Your brain then compares this new experience to those old memories. formal: I 'm going to go off the assumption that you do n't know what tor is , if you do then feel free to skip the next paragraph . Taking the information from the servers of the website to the ISP 's servers and then back to my computer . casual:

Normally, if I open Firefox and go to Reddit, my computer asks for a specific piece of info. That request goes from my computer straight to my internet provider's servers, then on to Reddit's servers, and they send back the webpage. It's like a direct line. But Tor messes with that. Instead of going directly from me to Reddit, it first encrypts *everything* – meaning it scrambles all the messages. Then, it bounces those encrypted messages around through these different Tor nodes before actually asking for the data.

formal: Much misinformation regarding this , Do n't think of sovereign debt as similar to household debt , it 's not . Looking at how things have grown in the past, most experts think we could handle around $480 billion in debt growth each year (that’s about 3%!), and it wouldn't be a big deal.
